why: Lucky Louis says the indexer keeps re-selecting the same positions. The other two are hypotheses about the bytes inside entries.
title: Neighbour similarity

q: Which property is established, and which are hypotheses?
a: Lucky Louis is established (HiSparse measured it); fallen-apple and upstairs similarity are hypotheses
wrong: Fallen-apple is established; Lucky Louis is a hypothesis
why: HiSparse measured selection reuse on a real trace. Nobody has measured how many bits a neighbouring entry saves at 8-bit precision.
title: Neighbour similarity

q: Neighbour similarity along the token axis compares entry E[l, t] with…
a: An entry of the same layer, some tokens earlier, E[l, t − Δ]
wrong: The same token one layer down, E[l − 1, t]
Another head’s slice of the same entry
The query of the current step
why: The token axis is the fallen-apple member of the family; the layer axis is the upstairs member.
title: Neighbour similarity

q: In what unit is neighbour similarity measured on this site?
a: Bits per element saved when the neighbour is known, H(E) − H(E | neighbour)
wrong: Cosine similarity between the two entries
why: Bits × entry size = bytes on the link, which is what the proposal must save. Cosine and perplexity do not convert to bytes.
title: Neighbour similarity

q: Why is cosine similarity not a good measure for this project?
a: Two entries can point the same way and still cost almost full price to store exactly given each other
wrong: Cosine similarity is always close to zero for KV entries
Cosine similarity cannot be computed for 8-bit numbers
Cosine similarity ignores the first channel
why: Cosine can be dominated by a few large channels; lossless coding pays for every element, including the many that the neighbour does not predict (IV.8 has an example).
title: Neighbour similarity

q: What does fallen-apple similarity claim?
a: An entry is cheaper to store exactly given an entry of the same layer a small token distance away — and the closer, the cheaper
wrong: Entries inside one block are identical
The indexer keeps selecting nearby entries
The model tolerates 2-bit keys without loss of accuracy
why: It is a statement about the conditional entropy H(Et​∣Et−Δ​) as a function of the token distance Δ.
title: Fallen-apple similarity

q: Why is fallen-apple similarity defined as a curve over Δ rather than “similar within a block”?
a: Because the block size is our knob; the data only has distances, and the right block size is read off the curve
wrong: Because blocks are too small to measure
Because curves are easier to plot than thresholds
Because the GPU cannot store blocks
why: A threshold at b would bake our design choice into the hypothesis. A curve over Δ tells us which b would pay.
title: Fallen-apple similarity

q: Is fallen-apple similarity established by HiSparse’s high hit rate?
a: No — the hit rate is about which entries are selected, not about their bytes
wrong: Yes — a high hit rate means entries are alike
Yes, for blocks larger than 4096 tokens
why: That is the Lucky Louis property. IV.13 shows hit rates like HiSparse’s coming from keys that cannot be compressed by a single bit.
title: Fallen-apple similarity

q: “Keys can be quantized to 2 bits with little loss in accuracy.” What does that say about fallen-apple similarity?
a: Nothing directly — it is about what the model tolerates, not about what is predictable
wrong: That keys compress losslessly to 2 bits
why: Lossy tolerance and lossless predictability are different questions. Lossless coding must reproduce every bit, including the ones the model would not miss.
title: Fallen-apple similarity

q: Two 640-element entries share four huge channels and are independent elsewhere. Their cosine similarity is 0.86. How much does one help to store the other exactly?
a: Almost nothing — 636 of the 640 elements are unpredictable from it
wrong: All the bits — the entries are near-copies
why: Cosine is dominated by the few large channels. Lossless coding pays for every element, and the neighbour explains none of the other 636.
title: Fallen-apple similarity

q: What does upstairs similarity claim?
a: The entry of the same token one layer up is partly predictable from the entry below it
wrong: Later tokens are predictable from earlier tokens of the same layer
The indexer selects the same positions in adjacent layers
why: H(El+1,t​∣El,t​)<H(El+1,t​) — the neighbour is along the layer axis, same token.
title: Upstairs similarity

q: In the building picture, what are the floors and what are the windows?
a: Floors are layers; windows along each floor are token positions
wrong: Floors are tokens; windows are layers
Floors are heads; windows are channels
Floors are blocks; windows are requests
why: Upstairs = same window, next floor up. Fallen-apple = same floor, a few windows along.
title: Upstairs similarity

q: What would strong upstairs similarity allow?
a: One dictionary shared by a group of adjacent layers, so fewer dictionaries to store, load and keep resident
wrong: Skipping the indexer at every second layer
Dropping the upper layers’ entries entirely
A larger hot cache at no cost
why: With groups of g layers sharing a dictionary, a block needs about 78/g dictionaries instead of 78 in the reference setting.
title: Upstairs similarity

q: Why is upstairs similarity second priority?
a: The proposal works without it; it would only make dictionaries cheaper to share
why: Per-layer block dictionaries need only fallen-apple similarity. Cross-layer sharing is an optimisation on top.
title: Upstairs similarity

q: What is a heavy block?
a: A block that holds many of the current step’s selections
wrong: A block whose dictionary is large
A block whose entries have large values
why: Heavy is about traffic, not size. If selections pile into a few heavy blocks for many steps, their dictionaries are cheap to keep on the GPU.
title: Lucky Louis, block by block

q: How does the block form of the Lucky Louis property differ from the ordinary one?
a: The ordinary one says the same entries are re-selected; the block form says selections also crowd into a few blocks that stay busy for many steps
wrong: The block form is about the bytes inside entries
The block form is about the layer axis
why: Selections can repeat while being scattered over the whole history. Then each miss tends to land in a different block, and a few resident dictionaries help little.
title: Lucky Louis, block by block

q: One dictionary load costs about as much link traffic as how many raw misses?
a: w — its weight in entries’ worth
why: A load moves we bytes, a raw miss e. Against about 274 misses per layer per step, loads × w must stay well below 274.
title: Lucky Louis, block by block

q: When does the heavy-block question stop mattering?
a: When dictionaries are light enough to keep every block’s dictionary resident
wrong: When the hot cache is larger than 8192 slots
When the indexer selects fewer entries
Never — it always decides the outcome
why: A 100K-token request in blocks of 4096 has 25 blocks per layer; at w=2 all their dictionaries take 50 entries’ worth, about 1 % of a 4096-slot hot cache.
title: Lucky Louis, block by block

q: What are the three rungs of the cat-thread ladder, from top to bottom?
a: An entry against everything, against its thread, against its surrounding block
wrong: Against its layer, its head, its channel
Against the hot cache, host memory, the link
why: Each rung narrows what the entry is compared with — and so, intuitively, makes it less surprising.
title: The cat-thread ladder

q: What is “the jump” at the end of the cat-thread argument?
a: Concluding from HiSparse’s high hit rate that the bottom rung is steep, so block dictionaries will work
wrong: Concluding that cats and dogs need different models
Concluding that the thread rung is useless
Concluding that the hot cache should be larger
why: The jump uses evidence about which entries are selected as if it were evidence about how alike their bytes are. IV.13 takes it apart.
title: The cat-thread ladder

q: Which parts of the cat-thread argument survive scrutiny?
a: Its direction (a theorem), its unit (bits) and the reality of shared subjects; the jump does not, and the size of the gain is harsh
why: IV.12 keeps what is right, IV.13 shows the leak in the jump, IV.14 prices the rungs with the exchange rate.
title: The cat-thread ladder

q: Why is H(E)≥H(E∣thread)≥H(E∣block) guaranteed?
a: Conditioning never increases entropy on average, and knowing the block also tells you the thread
wrong: Because blocks are smaller than threads
It is not guaranteed; it is a hypothesis
why: Side information can only help on average (II.5). The block rung refines the thread rung, so it can only help further.
title: What the ladder gets right

q: The ladder’s direction is a theorem. What is NOT guaranteed?
a: How big each step down is — it can be zero
wrong: That the bottom rung is lower than the top
That bits are the right unit
why: In the toy, set both “differ by” sliders to zero: all three rungs are equal. The theorem gives the direction; only data gives the size.
title: What the ladder gets right

q: “Redundancy”, “similarity” and “predictability” — how many different quantities are these on this site?
a: One — the mutual information, in bits
wrong: Two: one in bits, one as a percentage
None of them can be measured
why: All three are H(E)−H(E∣⋅), the bits saved by knowing something — and bits × entry size = bytes on the link.
title: What the ladder gets right

q: What kind of dictionary captures “sameness of subject” between entries of the same passage?
a: A location dictionary — the typical value of each channel in that passage
wrong: A list of repeated byte strings
A copy of the hot cache
why: Entries about the same subject have typical values that sit closer together; storing those typical values once lets each entry be stored as a smaller difference.
title: What the ladder gets right

q: What does a high hot-cache hit rate tell us?
a: That the query ranks the history at step t+1 much as it did at step t
wrong: That neighbouring entries hold similar numbers
That the model’s keys are low-rank
why: Hits need stable rankings, and stable rankings need a slowly moving query. Nothing about the keys resembling each other is required.
title: The leak: hit rate is about queries

q: In the live Monte Carlo, the keys are drawn independently at random. How well does a key predict the next one?
a: Not at all — R² ≈ 0.000, so a neighbour saves no bits
wrong: It depends on the query drift
why: Independent keys share nothing. Yet with a slowly drifting query, overlap and hit rate look like HiSparse’s.
title: The leak: hit rate is about queries

q: What controls the hit rate in the toy: the query drift η or the similarity of neighbouring keys?
a: The query drift η
wrong: Neither — it is fixed by k
why: Switching to keys that are close copies of their neighbours (R² ≈ 0.9) leaves the hit-rate curve almost unchanged; moving η changes it completely.
title: The leak: hit rate is about queries

q: Can a history compress well and still cache badly?
a: Yes — near-identical keys with a fast-moving query
wrong: No — compressible histories always cache well
Only if the hot cache is tiny
why: The two properties are produced by different things — the keys’ statistics and the query’s motion — and either can hold without the other.
title: The leak: hit rate is about queries

q: A predictor explains 75 % of an element’s variance. How many bits per element does it save (Gaussian exchange rate)?
a: 1 bit
why: 21​log2​1−R21​=21​log2​4=1. Two bits need 94 %.
title: The trap: the exchange rate is harsh

q: With the budget 30 % global, 20 % thread, 20 % block, 30 % noise, what is the block rung alone worth?
a: About 0.37 bit per element
why: 21​log2​0.31​−21​log2​0.51​≈0.87−0.50=0.37. The whole ladder is worth about 0.87 bit.
title: The trap: the exchange rate is harsh

q: To save one full bit per element from the block rung alone, how much of the variance left by the thread rung must the block explain?
a: Three quarters of it
why: The rung saves ½ log₂ of the ratio of residual variances before and after it; one bit needs that ratio to be 4.
title: The trap: the exchange rate is harsh

q: Why can a few near-deterministic channels save more than their share suggests?
a: The exchange rate rises steeply as R² approaches 1, so a channel with 2 % noise saves about 2.8 bits
wrong: Because large channels are stored with more bits
Because the noise floor does not apply to them
why: Bits per element are an average over channels. ½ log₂(1/0.02) ≈ 2.8 bits on a tenth of the channels adds about 0.28 bit to the average on its own.
title: The trap: the exchange rate is harsh

q: How many concurrent decode requests can one GPU serve, in this site’s model?
a: N=min(Nlink​,NHBM​) — the lower of what the link can feed and what GPU memory can hold
wrong: Nlink​+NHBM​
max(Nlink​,NHBM​)
Nlink​×NHBM​
why: Each request needs its misses delivered over the link and its hot cache held in GPU memory; whichever runs out first sets the count.
title: What "better than HiSparse" means

q: In the reference setting, which ceiling binds for HiSparse at B = 4096, and which at B = 8192?
a: The link at 4096 (about 110 vs 146); GPU memory at 8192 (about 73 vs 219)
why: Doubling the hot cache halves the misses (link relief) but doubles the memory per request.
title: What "better than HiSparse" means

q: What does lever 1 change, and which ceiling does it lift?
a: Misses move ρ·e instead of e bytes, lifting the link ceiling by up to 1/ρ
wrong: Slots hold deltas, lifting the memory ceiling
why: Lever 1 is the first variant of kv-blockdiff — δ-misses. Lever 2 stores hot-cache entries as deltas, which lifts the memory ceiling or buys a bigger cache.
title: What "better than HiSparse" means

q: Why do the two levers compound to roughly ρ² in miss traffic?
a: A cache of compressed slots holds 1/ρ times more entries, so about ρ times fewer misses; and each miss is ρ times smaller
wrong: Because ρ is applied to keys and to values
Because both levers use the same dictionary twice
Because the link is used in both directions
why: The miss rate falls roughly as B−1.08, so growing B by 1/ρ cuts misses by about ρ. For ρ=0.65: traffic falls about 2.4×.
title: What "better than HiSparse" means

q: Which metric comes first in the plan, and which is the headline?
a: Bits per element of the lossless code comes first; requests per GPU versus HiSparse is the headline
wrong: Kernel latency comes first; perplexity is the headline
Hit rate comes first; bits per element is the headline
Requests per GPU comes first; hit rate is the headline
why: Bits per element (ρ × 8) is the scientific number; f_D and dictionary loads come from trace replay; requests per GPU is the engineering result.
title: What "better than HiSparse" means

q: Which data path does this project care about?
a: The sparse-decode miss path — scattered single entries that must each decode alone
wrong: The bulk transfer of a whole prompt’s KV from the prefill GPU to the decode GPU
The network fetch of a stored prefix from another machine
The KV cache kept compressed in GPU memory and decoded at every attention step
why: Per layer per step the hot cache misses about 274 scattered 640-byte entries in the reference setting; each one must be rebuilt on its own, given only what is already on the GPU.
title: How we read papers

q: Why can a codec that is excellent for bulk transfer still be the wrong shape for the miss path?
a: It may only decode a whole stream front to back, so one entry cannot be rebuilt alone
wrong: Bulk codecs cannot run on a GPU
Bulk transfers move fewer bytes than the miss path
why: The access pattern decides the form. A stream coder carries state from one value to the next; the miss path needs random access to single entries.
title: How we read papers

q: A lossy paper shows that keys survive rounding to 2 bits. What does that tell us about lossless coding?
a: Little — it is a statement about the model’s tolerance, not about how predictable the stored bits are
wrong: That keys can be stored losslessly in 2 bits
That keys have an entropy of 2 bits per element
That values cannot be compressed at all
why: Lossless savings are set by how much of each number a predictor explains. A model can tolerate coarse rounding of numbers that are, bit for bit, unpredictable.
title: How we read papers

q: KV-Codec reports “lossless accuracy”. What does that mean in this site’s words?
a: The model’s answers did not get worse — the KV numbers were still rounded first, so the scheme is lossy
wrong: Every bit of the BF16 cache comes back unchanged
The video coder needs no prediction
Accuracy goes up as compression goes up
why: KV-Codec rounds KV to integers and then codes those integers losslessly. The integers come back exactly; the original BF16 numbers do not.
title: How we read papers

q: SplitZip calls its table of the 16 most frequent exponents a “codebook”. What is it in this site’s words?
a: A fixed-length code with escapes, fit once on calibration data and shared by every request
wrong: A separate dictionary for every block of tokens
A probability table that an arithmetic coder updates as it reads
why: On this site “codebook” means VQ centroids only. SplitZip’s table maps the 16 common exponent values to 4-bit codewords; everything else goes to the escape stream.
title: How we read papers

q: What does HiSparse change about decoding?
a: Where entries live — host memory or GPU memory — and nothing about their values
wrong: The numbers stored in each entry
How many entries attention reads per step
why: HiSparse moves raw entries between host DRAM and a small LRU hot cache in HBM. Attention reads the same entries with the same bytes, so the model’s outputs are unchanged.
title: HiSparse (2026)

q: At a hot cache of 4096 slots, LRU misses 13.4 % of selections and Bélády’s clairvoyant policy 8.2 %. What does the gap tell us?
a: A perfect eviction policy would remove only about 5 points of misses — the eviction lever is nearly used up
wrong: LRU is a poor policy and should be replaced
Doubling the cache would not reduce misses
Bélády’s policy can be built from the indexer’s scores
why: Bélády’s policy knows the future, so no real policy can beat it. To cut misses much further you need a bigger cache, or cheaper misses.
title: HiSparse (2026)

q: How many traces are HiSparse’s locality numbers (30 / 13.4 / 6.7 % misses) measured on?
a: One — a single 100,384-token LongBenchV2 prompt on GLM-5.1, averaged over decode steps
why: The trace is one request with 1,799 decode steps over 78 sparse layers. The means cover the first 1,000 steps.
title: HiSparse (2026)

q: The power law m(B) ∝ B^−1.08 through HiSparse’s points rests on what?
a: Three points at evenly spaced cache sizes — so the fitted slope is set by the two end points alone
wrong: A thousand cache sizes simulated from the trace
A fit over six different models
why: For three evenly spaced points, the least-squares slope equals the slope between the first and the last. Through the two larger caches alone the exponent is 1.00.
title: HiSparse (2026)

q: Why may the 30 % point at B = k be fitted together with the LRU points?
a: With exactly k slots, LRU must hold this step’s k selections, so it is the same as keeping only the current top-k
wrong: Because it was measured on a different model
Because Bélády’s policy equals LRU at that size
It may not; it is a different policy
why: When the cache has exactly k slots and all k selections must be resident, nothing else can stay. “LRU at B = k” and “top-k only” are one policy.
title: HiSparse (2026)

q: What do DSA, NSA, Quest and CSA have in common that our design relies on?
a: Each announces, per layer, which positions attention will read before any KV bytes are touched
wrong: Each picks single tokens one by one
Each must be trained together with the model
Each stores the KV cache in compressed form
why: That announcement is the demand signal a hot cache, or a delta store, serves. Everything else about the selectors can differ.
title: Sparse-attention selectors: DSA, NSA, Quest, CSA

q: How does Quest score a page of positions without reading every key in it?
a: It keeps each channel’s smallest and largest key value in the page and computes an upper bound of the query–key score
wrong: It reads one trained summary key per page
It averages the keys of the page
It reuses the previous step’s attention weights
why: For each channel, whichever end (min or max) gives the larger product with the query’s element bounds every key in the page; summing over channels bounds the whole score.
title: Sparse-attention selectors: DSA, NSA, Quest, CSA

q: Under DeepSeek-V4’s CSA, what is one “entry” that attention reads?
a: One learned compression of 4 consecutive tokens — fewer, larger units than tokens
wrong: One token, exactly as in DSA
The keys of one head only
why: CSA merges every 4 tokens into one compressed entry and lets its indexer pick the top 512 (Flash) or 1024 (Pro) of those.
title: Sparse-attention selectors: DSA, NSA, Quest, CSA

q: Why does a selector that picks pages or blocks help a design built on block dictionaries?
a: Its picks come in runs of consecutive positions, so misses pile into fewer blocks
wrong: It makes neighbouring entries more alike
why: Fewer distinct blocks per step means fewer dictionaries that must be resident on the GPU — the heavy-block question is partly answered by the selector’s design.
title: Sparse-attention selectors: DSA, NSA, Quest, CSA

q: Which part of each BF16 number does SplitZip store uncompressed?
a: The sign and the 7 mantissa bits — one raw byte per number
wrong: Nothing: every bit goes through the 4-bit code
why: The mantissa’s low bits are close to noise, so SplitZip keeps that byte as it is and codes only the exponent byte.
title: SplitZip (2026)

q: In SplitZip, what happens to an exponent that is not one of the 16 most frequent values?
a: It is escaped — its position and raw value go to a separate escape stream
wrong: It is rounded to the nearest frequent exponent
The whole tensor falls back to raw BF16
A new table is trained for that request
why: Rounding would make the coder lossy. The escape stream patches the rare values back in, at a cost of several dozen bits each.
title: SplitZip (2026)

q: Escapes aside, what is the most a 4-bit exponent code can shrink BF16 numbers?
wrong: 2×, because half the bits are exponent
why: Each number keeps 8 raw bits (sign and mantissa) and spends 4 on the exponent code, so 16 bits become at least 12. SplitZip’s measured 1.324× sits right under that ceiling.
title: SplitZip (2026)

q: Why does SplitZip’s 3-bit top-8 code expand E4M3 data instead of shrinking it?
a: It saves only 1 bit of the 4-bit exponent, and the escapes for uncovered values cost more than that
wrong: E4M3 values cannot be split into bytes
The mantissa grows when the exponent is coded
why: Even at 96 % coverage, 4 % of values × several dozen bits per escape is more than the 1 bit per value the code saves.
title: SplitZip (2026)

q: What actually stands between SplitZip’s format and decoding one entry on its own?
a: Its escape list — the 4-bit codes sit at known addresses, but you must look up whether an element was escaped
wrong: Coder state carried from value to value, as in arithmetic coding
Its need for a per-request dictionary
why: A fixed-length stream is addressable by construction. A small escape index per entry or per block would make the format random-access.
title: SplitZip (2026)

q: Draw numbers from one bell curve and store them in BF16. About how many bits of information does the 8-bit exponent field carry?
a: About 2.5 bits
why: Most values fall in a few binades around the curve’s width; the exponent’s entropy works out to 2.54 bits. That leaves about 5.5 of its 8 bits as redundancy for a coder to remove.
title: ZipNN, DFloat11 and friends

q: Why does LZ4, a byte-string matcher, shrink BF16 tensors by only about 2 %?
a: Floats almost never repeat as exact byte strings; their redundancy is in the uneven use of exponent values
wrong: LZ4 cannot run on a GPU
why: LZ matching copies earlier byte strings. Model numbers share a skewed exponent distribution, not repeated strings, so an entropy coder finds what LZ cannot.
title: ZipNN, DFloat11 and friends

q: DFloat11 reaches 1.42× on SplitZip’s KV workload and SplitZip 1.32×. What explains most of the gap?
a: DFloat11 entropy-codes the exponent (Huffman); SplitZip spends a fixed 4 bits on it for speed and simple addressing
wrong: DFloat11 uses a dictionary per block of tokens
why: Variable-length codewords approach the exponent’s entropy; a fixed-length code pays a little more per value in exchange for parallel decoding and known addresses.
title: ZipNN, DFloat11 and friends

q: ZipNN’s 1.515× in SplitZip’s comparison table is suspicious for which reason?
a: It beats the ceiling of any exponent-only coder on that workload (about 1.42× at 3.29 bits of exponent entropy)
wrong: ZipNN does not code exponents at all
why: With 8 raw bits of sign and mantissa, 3.29 bits of exponent gives 16 / 11.29 ≈ 1.42×. Either ZipNN squeezes the other byte too, or its number was measured on other data.
title: ZipNN, DFloat11 and friends

q: In KV-Codec’s layout, what does the previous video frame hold, relative to the current one?
a: The neighbouring token — so predicting from the previous frame is predicting an entry from the token before it
wrong: Another attention head of the same token
why: Frames follow the token axis. A video coder’s favourite move, “same place, one frame back”, becomes fallen-apple prediction at token distance 1.
title: KV-Codec (2026)

q: Which step of KV-Codec throws information away?
a: Rounding the KV numbers to integers before the video coder sees them
wrong: The H.265 coder in lossless mode
Decoding on the GPU’s video chip
why: The video coder is run in its lossless mode, so the integers come back exactly; the original BF16 numbers do not. “Lossless accuracy” means the benchmark scores did not drop.
title: KV-Codec (2026)

q: Swapping half of the numbers between attention heads made KV-Codec’s ratio 2.4× worse. What does that show?
a: Which numbers sit next to each other inside a frame decides how well a neighbour-predicting coder works
wrong: Heads are identical to each other
why: The swap leaves the token order alone and scrambles each frame’s picture, so much of the ratio must come from structure inside one token’s numbers.
title: KV-Codec (2026)

q: Why is KV-Codec only weak evidence for fallen-apple similarity?
a: Its ratio mixes rounding with coding and does not separate prediction from the previous frame from prediction within a frame
wrong: It measures the layer axis, not the token axis
It reports no compression ratio at all
It shuffles the tokens before coding
why: To isolate the token axis you would turn off prediction from earlier frames, or shuffle the token order, and see how much the ratio falls. We found neither in what we could read.
title: KV-Codec (2026)

q: KIVI rounds keys “per channel”. In this site’s words, which numbers share one rounding ruler?
a: One channel — one element position — across a run of tokens (a column)
wrong: All the numbers of one token’s key vector (a row)
All keys of one layer at once
One head’s keys and values together
why: A channel is one fixed element position looked at across many vectors. Per-channel rounding computes the ruler (smallest value and step) over tokens, separately for each position.
title: KIVI (2024)

q: In the toy key table, why does a per-token ruler ruin the small channels?
a: Each row’s ruler must also span the two big channels, so its step is too coarse for the small numbers
wrong: Because the small channels drift over time
Because 2 bits cannot store negative numbers
Because per-token rounding ignores the big channels
why: A row holds values from about −9 to +12, so four marks are 6 to 7 apart and no mark sits near the small numbers. A column of small numbers gets a ruler of its own.
title: KIVI (2024)

q: Counting a 16-bit smallest value and a 16-bit step per scale group of 32 numbers, what does “2-bit” KIVI cost per number?
a: About 3 bits
why: 2 bits of code plus 32 bits of ruler shared by 32 numbers = 1 more bit each. This is our count, under the stated assumption about how the ruler is stored.
title: KIVI (2024)

q: KIVI shows that keys survive 2-bit rounding. What does that tell us about an exact (lossless) copy of 8-bit keys?
a: Little — it is about what the model tolerates, not about how much of each number is predictable
wrong: That 8-bit keys compress losslessly to about 2 bits
That keys have no noise below the second bit
why: Rounding throws away the six low bits; a lossless coder must reproduce them, noise included. What it can save depends on the variance a predictor explains, which KIVI does not report.
title: KIVI (2024)

q: Which of our dictionaries is KIVI’s per-channel key ruler a lossy cousin of?
a: A per-channel location and scale shared by a block of tokens
wrong: A pointer to the nearest sibling entry
why: Per channel, per 32 tokens, KIVI keeps a smallest value and a step — a location and a scale. Our lightest dictionary keeps the same two numbers per channel, but uses them to predict, not to round.
title: KIVI (2024)

q: Why are keys easier to round per channel before RoPE than after it?
a: RoPE turns each pair of channels by an angle that grows with position, so a channel with a steady large value starts to swing
wrong: RoPE adds random noise to every key
RoPE makes all channels the same size
why: Before RoPE a channel can sit near 9 token after token; after RoPE the same number is shared between the two channels of its pair in proportions that change with position.
title: KVQuant (2024)

q: KVQuant’s “dense-and-sparse” step stores the largest ~1 % of numbers separately. Which idea from this site is that?
a: Escapes — rare values stored in full, with their positions, outside the fixed-width code
why: The rest of the vector then needs a much narrower ruler. Fixed-length codes with an escape stream make the same trade.
title: KVQuant (2024)

q: According to KVQuant’s appendix, if keys are rounded per token (not per channel), is rounding before RoPE still better?
a: No — with per-token rulers, rounding after RoPE did better
wrong: Yes, always, by a wide margin
It makes no difference at all
The paper did not try per-token rulers
why: LLaMA-7B, 3-bit uniform, per-token: perplexity 10.87 after RoPE versus 14.68 before (16-bit: 5.68). Pre-RoPE pays off only together with per-channel rulers.
title: KVQuant (2024)

q: If we store keys before RoPE, what changes for a lossless coder?
a: The exact target becomes the 8-bit pre-RoPE keys, and the GPU must apply RoPE after reading them back
wrong: Nothing at all; RoPE is exactly invertible in any number format
Values must also be stored before RoPE
why: In floating point a rotation is not bit-exactly undone, so “store pre-RoPE” is a design choice made up front, not a free re-encoding of post-RoPE keys.
title: KVQuant (2024)

q: Which running theme does KVQuant’s non-uniform grid illustrate?
a: The number grid is not neutral
wrong: Which entries, versus what is inside them
why: Where the marks sit decides which numbers are cheap; for us the grid is fixed by the storage format (E4M3 or INT8), and it changes what prediction can save.
title: KVQuant (2024)

q: In this site’s vocabulary, what is the “PCA decorrelation” step of KVTC?
a: A KLT — a rotation onto the axes along which the data spreads most, fitted once on calibration data
why: PCA and the KLT are the same mathematics. KVTC fits the axes once, offline, and reuses them for every cache — a global-scope dictionary.
title: KVTC (2026)

q: How does a lossy transform coder like KVTC reach ratios like 20×?
a: It gives zero bits to the many small components below a “water level” and drops them
wrong: It codes every component exactly with fewer bits
why: Bits go to a component in proportion to the log of its variance above the water level; below it, nothing is stored at all.
title: KVTC (2026)

q: What does the same rotation save in a lossless coder?
a: The transform coding gain, ½ log₂ (AM/GM) of the variances, in bits per number
wrong: The same ratio as the lossy coder
Nothing — rotations never help lossless coding
log₂ of the number of components dropped
why: A lossless coder cannot drop components; every one still costs bits down to the stored grid. Only the uneven spread of variance is saved, and only logarithmically.
title: KVTC (2026)

q: Why can a steep raw spectrum overstate what a rotation adds for us?
a: Part of the steepness is just channels of different sizes, which a per-channel code already prices in
wrong: Because PCA is inaccurate on GPUs
Because the spectrum is measured on values only
why: Big channels (KIVI’s observation) make a few raw variances large. A per-channel location and scale capture that without rotating; the rotation’s own gain is measured on standardized data.
title: KVTC (2026)

q: Why is KVTC’s final packing step (DEFLATE) fine for KVTC and wrong for our miss path?
a: DEFLATE is a stream coder; KVTC compresses whole caches, we read single scattered entries
why: A stream must be decoded from its start. Offloading a whole cache reads it all anyway; the sparse-decode miss path reads a few hundred bytes from anywhere.
title: KVTC (2026)

q: What is sparse coding, in one sentence?
a: Describing a vector as a weighted sum of a few atoms chosen from a large fixed dictionary, storing only which atoms and their weights
wrong: Storing only the non-zero elements of a vector
Rotating a vector onto its principal axes
why: VQ is the special case of one atom with weight 1; a KLT uses every axis with a weight.
title: Lexico (2024)

q: With 8 atoms per vector, a dictionary of 4096 atoms and 8-bit weights, how many bits does one vector cost?
a: 160 bits — 8 × (12 index bits + 8 weight bits)
why: Naming one of 4096 atoms takes log₂ 4096 = 12 bits. A 128-number vector at 16 bits is 2048 bits, so 160 bits is about 8 % of it.
title: Lexico (2024)

q: For a lossless coder using Lexico-like atoms (8 per vector, 4096 in the dictionary, 8-bit weights, 128 numbers per vector), what share of variance must the atoms explain just to break even?
a: About 82 %
why: The tax is 160 bits / 128 numbers = 1.25 bits per number; ½ log₂ 1/(1−R²) = 1.25 needs 1−R² = 2^−2.5 ≈ 0.18.
title: Lexico (2024)

q: In the toy, why does the net lossless gain fall after the third atom?
a: Later atoms only fit noise — they explain little variance but each still pays the full tax
wrong: Because the dictionary runs out of atoms
Because OMP picks atoms at random
why: The vector was built from three atoms plus noise. Once those are found, more atoms add a few percent of explained variance and 15 bits of tax each.
title: Lexico (2024)

q: What does Lexico’s success with one dictionary per model suggest for kv-blockdiff?
a: That a global dictionary, fitted once and shared by every request, is a real rung of the ladder — free at serving time
why: It is evidence that much structure is shared by all texts. It cannot say how much a request’s or a block’s own dictionary adds on top.
title: Lexico (2024)

q: In CacheGen, what is each non-anchor token stored as?
a: Its difference from the first token of its group of 10 (the anchor), same layer and channel
wrong: Its difference from the immediately preceding token
Its difference from the layer below
why: Referencing one shared anchor lets all nine differences be computed and decoded in parallel. The first draft of this proposal said “adjacent-token deltas”; that was not quite right.
title: CacheGen (2024)

q: CacheGen’s arithmetic coder uses a separate probability table per (layer, channel). In this site’s words, what is that?
a: Per-channel histograms — the context-free per-channel code
why: CacheGen found that grouping numbers by channel and layer lowers entropy more than grouping by token position — the same reason a global per-channel code is our baseline.
title: CacheGen (2024)

q: Subtracting a neighbour that carries its own independent noise does what to the noise variance?
a: Doubles it
why: The difference of two numbers with independent noise of variance σ² has noise variance 2σ². Differencing pays off only when slow drift dominates the fast noise.
title: CacheGen (2024)

q: If the deltas’ 2.4× smaller variance is measured against each channel’s own typical value, at least how much of a channel’s variance must be slow drift?
a: About 79 %
why: The difference keeps at least twice the noise, so 2(1−f) ≤ 1/2.4, which gives f ≥ 0.79.
title: CacheGen (2024)

q: CacheGen’s anchor groups have the shape of which kv-blockdiff object?
a: A block of 10 tokens whose dictionary is one entry (the anchor)
why: Every token is rebuilt from the anchor plus its own difference — a block dictionary of weight 1 with b = 10. The arithmetic coder then turns each chunk into a stream.
title: CacheGen (2024)

q: What does KVComp’s “cache-resident decompression” mean, in plain words?
a: Decoded numbers go straight from fast on-chip memory into the attention dot products, never written back to GPU main memory
wrong: The cache is decompressed once at the start of decoding
Only the hot cache is compressed
why: Writing decoded numbers back to GPU memory and reading them again would cost the very bandwidth compression saves.
title: KVComp (2025)

q: Which of KVComp’s choices are KIVI’s ruler directions?
a: Keys rounded with per-channel rulers in blocks of tokens, values with per-token rulers
wrong: Keys per token, values per channel
why: Same observation — key channels have sizes of their own, values vary by token — used before a Huffman coder.
title: KVComp (2025)

q: In the grid figure (R² = 75 %), how does a predictor’s saving change from an 8-bit-like grid (σ = 32 steps) to a coarse one (σ = 1 step)?
a: Fewer bits saved (1.00 → 0.69) but a larger share of the total (14 % → 33 %)
wrong: More bits saved and a larger share
why: A coarse grid shrinks every cost, the predictor’s saving included, but the order-0 cost shrinks faster. The grid alone does not make predictors useless.
title: KVComp (2025)

q: Why might a predictor really not pay in KVComp’s setting?
a: Its block-wise per-channel rulers already absorb the simplest predictable part, and a predictor would add work inside every attention step
wrong: Because Huffman codes cannot code residuals
Because KV caches have no structure
why: A ruler per channel per block is a location and scale — exactly what the simplest predictor would supply. What is left must be explained by something else.
title: KVComp (2025)

q: Which kv-blockdiff path needs the decoder speed KVComp demonstrates?
a: Lever 2, decoding compressed entries inside the attention read; lever 1 decodes only on misses
why: Lever 1 decodes a miss once and needs about 50 GB/s; lever 2 reads compressed slots every step, which is KVComp’s regime.
title: KVComp (2025)

q: The receiver knows Y, which equals X or differs from it in one of three bits. Without knowing Y, how many bits must the sender spend on X?
a: 2 bits — the index of X’s bin
wrong: 0 bits: the receiver can guess X from Y
why: Bins pair each 3-bit string with its complement. The two members differ in all three bits, so only one of them can be within one flip of Y.
title: The classics we lean on

q: In kv-blockdiff the encoder builds each block dictionary itself. What is the formal home of coding entries against it?
a: Ordinary conditional coding — both ends know the dictionary; Slepian–Wolf is needed only for side information the encoder cannot see
wrong: Slepian–Wolf coding, because only the GPU holds the dictionary
Wyner–Ziv coding, because the deltas are lossy
Rate–distortion theory with no side information
why: Slepian–Wolf’s surprise is that the sender may lack Y. When the sender has Y — our case for dictionaries — the classic H(X | Y) of Part II already applies.
title: The classics we lean on

q: Why can one pass over a trace give an LRU cache’s misses at every size at once?
a: A request misses exactly when its stack distance is at least the cache size, so counting distances answers every size
wrong: Because every cache size has the same miss rate
why: LRU’s contents at size B are always contained in its contents at size B + 1 (Mattson’s inclusion property), which is what makes the stack distance meaningful.
title: The classics we lean on

q: On the toy trace, LRU with 3 slots misses 7 times and Bélády’s policy 6 times. What does the 6 mean?
a: No eviction policy whatsoever can miss fewer than 6 times with 3 slots on this trace
wrong: LRU can be tuned to reach 6
Bélády’s policy is what HiSparse uses
why: Bélády’s policy knows the future and evicts the item needed furthest ahead; it is optimal for equal-cost misses, so it is a floor, not a design.
title: The classics we lean on

q: Why is the step x → x + round(a · y) exactly reversible on integers?
a: The step leaves y unchanged, so the decoder recomputes the same round(a · y) and subtracts it
wrong: Because rounding never changes an integer
Because a is always an integer
why: That is lifting. Three such shears make a rotation; a PLUS factorization makes any matrix with determinant ±1 out of such steps.
title: The classics we lean on

q: Which kind of evidence do the lossy KV papers (KIVI, KVQuant, KVTC, Lexico, CacheGen) give us?
a: Where structure lives and what the model tolerates — not how many bits an exact copy needs
why: Their yardsticks are accuracy and perplexity at a memory budget. Lossless gains are set by variance explained, which none of them reports.
title: What would be new

q: Which published coder measures KV redundancy in bits at 8 bits — and what is missing from it?
a: SplitZip — but only context-free (order-0): no neighbours, no dictionaries
why: SplitZip’s 6.19-bit order-0 bound on E5M2 is a bit count; it says nothing about how much a neighbour or a block dictionary would add.
title: What would be new

q: What is claim 1 of “what would be new”?
a: A measurement of neighbour similarity in bits per number, at 8-bit precision, with controls
wrong: A lossy compressor with a higher ratio
why: Fallen-apple and upstairs similarity in bits, with a shuffle control, a synthetic control and an exact round trip — publishable whether positive or negative.
title: What would be new

q: What is the honest caveat on claim 2, the random-access lossless delta store?
a: Its parts are known; only the combination and the target are new — and it is worth building only if claim 1 comes out positive
wrong: It has already been published by HiSparse
why: Fixed-length codes, escapes and block dictionaries all exist. If KV has no conditional structure at 8 bits, what remains is context-free coding on the miss path — useful, and less new.
title: What would be new

q: Why might the novelty claims be narrower than they look?
a: We checked papers through abstracts and summaries, and saw newer related titles we have not read
why: Being honest about the search is part of the claim. A measurement is still a result even if a neighbouring paper turns up.
title: What would be new

q: A bell-shaped channel stored in FP8 E4M3 has an order-0 entropy of about…
a: 6.47 bits per element, whatever the channel’s scale
wrong: 8 bits — every code is equally likely
4 bits — half the codes are never used
6.47 bits only for one particular scale
why: The E4M3 grid is logarithmic: scaling the channel slides its histogram along the codes without changing its shape, so the entropy stays at 6.47 bits (our Monte Carlo and the exact calculation agree).
title: The bit budget

q: Where do the 6.47 bits of an E4M3 element live?
a: About 1 bit of sign, 2.5 bits of exponent, 2.9 bits of mantissa
wrong: Mostly in the exponent — the mantissa is nearly free
8 bits spread evenly over all fields
why: The exponent is the only field with easy, context-free redundancy (4 bits stored, 2.5 bits of information). The mantissa is close to noise.
title: The bit budget

q: What does bpe count?
a: Bits per 8-bit element of a lossless code, with every cost included
wrong: Bits per entry, excluding the dictionary
The number of codes a channel uses
why: Residual bits, the per-entry side information and the dictionary spread over its block all count. Raw storage is 8, and ρ≈bpe/8.
title: The bit budget

q: Coding each element alone with a good fixed code can save at most about…
a: 1.5–1.8 bits per element (to 6.47 or 6.19 bits)
why: That is the gap between 8 bits and the order-0 entropy (6.47 for a Gaussian in E4M3, 6.19 measured by SplitZip on real E5M2 KV). A fixed-length code gets roughly 1 bit of it.
title: The bit budget

q: Where must everything a dictionary adds beyond that come from?
a: From conditional structure — other channels of the entry or other entries of the block making an element more predictable
why: An element’s own histogram is already used by the context-free code. Only information about the element that comes from elsewhere can lower its cost further.
title: The bit budget

q: What does solo coding use to code an element?
a: Only one fixed, global code per channel, fit once on calibration data
wrong: The previous entry of the same channel
A code fit to each request at prefill
why: The Hermit never looks at context. Its per-channel histograms are fit offline on a calibration corpus and shared by every request.
title: Solo coding: the Hermit

q: Roughly how much does solo coding save on 8-bit KV?
a: About 1.1–1.3× (0.8–1.8 bits per element)
why: The order-0 entropy is 6.2–6.5 bits (1.24–1.29× ideal); fixed-length versions reach about 1.10–1.14×. SplitZip’s top-8 code on real E4M3 even expanded the data (0.93×).
title: Solo coding: the Hermit

q: Why are all gains on this site counted from solo coding rather than from raw storage?
a: Because solo coding needs no dictionary, no residency and no block structure — any dictionary must beat it to be worth its costs
wrong: Because raw storage cannot be measured
Because solo coding is the slowest option
why: Solo coding is the free lunch already on the table. Counting from raw would credit a dictionary with savings it did not create.
title: Solo coding: the Hermit

q: A block’s values sit around a typical value of their own. The Hermit codes them with the global code. On average over blocks, how many extra bits does it pay per element?
a: ½ log₂ 1/(1 − R²), where R² is the share of variance the block means explain
wrong: Nothing — a global code is always optimal
One bit per element, whatever the drift
log₂ of the number of blocks
why: The extra cost of a wrong code is the gap between two distributions (a cross-entropy). Averaged over blocks it equals the exchange-rate formula — exactly what a location dictionary could win back.
title: Solo coding: the Hermit

q: A predictor explains R² = 75 % of an element’s variance. For bell-shaped data, how many bits per element does it save?
a: 1 bit
why: ½ log₂ 1/(1 − 0.75) = ½ log₂ 4 = 1. Two bits need 94 %, three bits need 98.4 %.
title: The exchange rate, applied

q: Starting from a context-free rate of 6.2 bits, what extra compression does a 75 % predictor give?
a: About 1.19×
why: 6.2 / (6.2 − 1) ≈ 1.19. Lossless gains stay modest unless the predictor explains nearly everything.
title: The exchange rate, applied

q: Which variance does R² refer to here?
a: The variance that remains after the context-free code, element by element
wrong: The variance of the whole cache
The variance of the attention scores
why: Bits are counted per element against the solo rate. A predictor must explain variance that the element’s own histogram does not already account for.
title: The exchange rate, applied

q: Ten channels of a 640-element entry are predicted almost perfectly (R² = 0.99, 3.3 bits each); the rest not at all. What is saved per element of the entry?
a: About 0.05 bit
why: Bits add up per element: 10 × 3.3 = 33 bits spread over 640 elements is 0.05 bit each. Owning most of the variance is not owning most of the bytes.
title: The exchange rate, applied

q: What are the three steps every lossless dictionary coder performs on an entry?
a: Predict it from the dictionary, take the exact integer residual, code the residual
wrong: Quantize it, round it, store the rounded value
Rotate it, drop the small coordinates, store the rest
Sort it, deduplicate it, compress it with zstd
why: Predict-then-correct. Exact integer residuals make the scheme lossless; how good the prediction is decides how small the residual is.
title: The shape of every dictionary coder

q: What is the per-entry tax?
a: Side information stored with every entry on top of its residual, such as which centroid or which sibling was used
wrong: The dictionary’s size divided by the block size
A fee for loading the dictionary onto the GPU
why: The dictionary is paid once per block (8w/b per element). The tax is paid again by every entry and travels with every miss.
title: The shape of every dictionary coder

q: A dictionary saves 0.40 bit per element on residuals, charges a 12-bit tax per 640-element entry, and weighs w = 64 entries’ worth over a block of b = 4096. Net saving?
a: About 0.26 bit per element
wrong: It loses about 0.1 bit per element
title: The shape of every dictionary coder

q: Which two costs travel with every miss on the link?
a: The residual bits and the per-entry tax — together they are the delta
why: The delta of an entry must decode alone given its dictionary, so it carries the residual and the tax. The dictionary is stored once per block and loaded or kept resident separately.
title: The shape of every dictionary coder

q: Which of the four dictionary types charges no per-entry tax at all?
a: loc, and the full KLT
why: loc predicts every entry with the same per-channel values; a full rotation replaces the entry by its rotated coordinates. VQ pays an index, sib a pointer, a partial KLT its coefficients.
title: The shape of every dictionary coder

q: What does a loc dictionary store?
a: For each channel, a location (typical value) and a scale (typical spread)
wrong: A rotation matrix for the block
A pointer to the most similar entry
why: Two numbers per channel, so about 2 entries’ worth: w≈2. Every entry is predicted by the same per-channel locations.
title: loc: the Anchor

q: What per-entry tax does loc charge?
a: None
why: The prediction is the same for every entry of the block, so nothing needs to be said per entry.
title: loc: the Anchor

q: A channel’s values have total variance 4 across all blocks and variance 1 inside each block. What does loc save on it?
a: 1 bit per element
wrong: Nothing — subtracting a constant never helps
why: ½ log₂(σ²_total / σ²_within) = ½ log₂ 4 = 1 bit. Block means explain 75 % of the variance.
title: loc: the Anchor

q: Why does subtracting one fixed, global location per channel save nothing for an ideal entropy coder?
a: Entropy does not depend on where a histogram sits, only on its shape
wrong: Because the location costs too many bytes
why: Shifting every value by the same constant leaves every probability unchanged. The Anchor’s gain comes from locations that change from block to block — drift. (A fixed-length code is different: there, centring narrows the code.)
title: loc: the Anchor

q: When does loc lose bits compared with solo coding?
a: Only by its own small dictionary cost (8 × 2 / b bits per element), or on the E4M3 grid when the prediction is poor
wrong: Whenever the data has no clusters
Whenever the block is longer than 1024 entries
Always, because it pays a per-entry tax
why: With no drift it gains nothing and pays 16/b bits per element — 0.004 bit at b = 4096. In E4M3 index space a poor prediction can cost more, which the per-channel flag of VI.11 catches.
title: loc: the Anchor

q: How much does a full KLT basis weigh for entries of d elements, stored in BF16?
a: 2d entries’ worth (d × d numbers at 2 bytes each)
why: An entry is d bytes at 8 bits per element; a d×d matrix in BF16 is 2d2 bytes =2d entries. For d=640 that is w=1280; a rank-16 partial basis is w=32.
title: KLT: the Compass, at work

q: What does a KLT save per element on bell-shaped data, before costs?
a: ½ log₂ (AM/GM) of the eigenvalues of the standardized covariance
wrong: ½ log₂ of the largest eigenvalue
why: The transform coding gain of II.16. AM/GM is 1 for a flat spectrum (no gain) and grows only when a few directions dominate.
title: KLT: the Compass, at work

q: 64 standardized channels: 8 directions with variance 10, the other 56 with variance 1. The KLT gain is about…
a: 0.34 bit per element
title: KLT: the Compass, at work

q: On the synthetic low-rank world (d = 64, b = 4096), the KLT gained 0.51 bit but netted only 0.26. Why?
a: Its full basis, charged to one block, cost 0.25 bit per element
wrong: Its per-entry tax ate the gain
why: 8w/b with w=2d+1=129 and b=4096 is 0.25. Fit once per request or globally, the same basis would cost almost nothing.
title: KLT: the Compass, at work

q: What per-entry tax does a VQ dictionary with C centroids charge?
a: log₂ C bits per entry, the index of the chosen centroid
why: The index tax of II.17. Spread over the d elements of an entry it is log2​C/d bits per element: 8/640 = 0.0125 for 256 centroids.
title: VQ: the Hive, at work

q: How much does a codebook of C = 256 full-size centroids cost per element when one block of b = 4096 entries pays for it?
a: 0.5 bit per element
why: 8C/b=8×256/4096=0.5. The codebook weighs w=C entries.
title: VQ: the Hive, at work

q: On bell-shaped (Gaussian) data, how does the best possible VQ compare with an untaxed rotation (KLT)?
a: It cannot beat it — its index buys at most log₂ C / d bits per element beyond the rotation, and that is exactly what the index costs
wrong: It always beats it, because centroids adapt to the data
They are equal only when C = 2
VQ wins when C is large enough
why: The rate–distortion bound. With its codebook charged too, VQ nets at most the KLT gain minus 8C/b.
title: VQ: the Hive, at work

q: In the Monte Carlo on correlated bell-shaped data (rank-8 signal, d = 64, b = 16,384), what did VQ net at best, against the KLT’s 0.50 bit?
a: About +0.22 bit
why: Our run gave +0.22 at C = 64 (the source draft reported up to +0.25). Larger codebooks gain more but pay more; at C = 4096 the net is about −1.3.
title: VQ: the Hive, at work

q: When did VQ clearly beat the rotation in the Monte Carlo?
a: On clustered data (32 real clusters) — +1.45 bits against +0.68
wrong: On the correlated Gaussian data at C = 4096
Only when the codebook was free
why: Codebooks earn their keep only when the data really clusters. Whether KV entries do is an empirical question.
title: VQ: the Hive, at work

q: What does a sib dictionary store, and what does it charge per entry?
a: Nothing beyond the block’s own entries; a pointer to the sibling, log₂ b bits per entry
wrong: C centroids; log₂ C bits per entry
One location per channel; no tax
why: The “dictionary” is the block itself. The pointer is cheap per element on long entries: 12 bits over 640 elements is 0.019.
title: sib: the Twin

q: Why does predicting an entry from a random sibling cost about half a bit per element more than predicting it from the block’s per-channel location?
a: The residual is the difference of two independent noises, so its variance doubles
wrong: Because the pointer costs half a bit
Because siblings are stored in E4M3
Because the sibling is from another block
why: Variances of independent parts add: 2σ² instead of σ². ½ log₂ 2 = 0.5 bit per element.
title: sib: the Twin

q: When does the Twin beat the Anchor on an entry?
a: When the entry has a near-duplicate whose shared part is bigger than the noise left in each
why: With a true twin the residual is only the two noises, variance 2σ²_noise, against the Anchor’s σ²_own + σ²_noise. That is smaller only when σ²_own > σ²_noise.
title: sib: the Twin

q: With d = 640 and b = 4096, choosing the nearest sibling instead of a random one brings the penalty against loc from +0.50 down to about…
a: +0.37 bit per element — still a loss
wrong: −0.5 — it beats loc by half a bit
why: In 640 dimensions all siblings are nearly equally far away, so the best of 4095 is only a little closer than a random one (our Monte Carlo).
title: sib: the Twin

q: What does the Twin need on the GPU at decode time that the other dictionaries do not?
a: The sibling entry itself, already decoded
why: Its prediction is another entry. That ties sib to residency — and two entries pointing at each other could never be decoded, so real schemes point at a few anchor entries.
title: sib: the Twin

q: Which dictionary types charge a per-entry tax?
a: VQ (log₂ C bits per entry) and sib (log₂ b bits per entry)
wrong: None of them — taxes are paid per block
why: loc and a full KLT predict every entry the same way, so nothing has to be said per entry. VQ must name a centroid, sib a sibling.
title: The four dictionaries side by side

q: Which dictionary is the heaviest, and where can it therefore live?
a: The full KLT basis (w = 2d) — it is affordable only when a whole request or all requests share it
wrong: sib — it stores the whole block
VQ with C = 16 — only per block
why: For d = 640, w = 1280 entries’ worth costs 2.5 bits per element when one block of 4096 pays for it.
title: The four dictionaries side by side

q: What do loc and the KLT have in common, and what separates them?
a: Both make one guess for every entry with no tax; loc looks at each channel alone, the KLT uses the other channels too
wrong: Both pay a tax per entry; loc’s is smaller
Both store centroids; the KLT’s are rotated
why: The Compass contains an Anchor (it centres before it rotates); what it adds is the correlation between channels.
title: The four dictionaries side by side

q: What do VQ and sib have in common, and what separates them?
a: Both choose a prediction per entry and pay to name it; VQ’s codebook is fit and paid for, sib’s codebook is the block itself
wrong: Both are taxless; VQ is larger
Both rotate the data; sib uses a smaller basis
Both need the sibling on the GPU
why: The Twin is a Hive with a free but noisy codebook — and both are bound by the same rate–distortion limit.
title: The four dictionaries side by side

q: On the five synthetic worlds, how many worlds did each dictionary type win?
a: One each — drift for loc, low rank for KLT, clusters for VQ, twins for sib — and on pure noise only loc stayed above zero
why: Each type is built to catch one kind of structure. Which kinds KV caches have is the measurement.
title: The four dictionaries side by side

q: What does the entropy rate measure?
a: What an ideal entropy coder (arithmetic coding, rANS) would pay for the residuals, plus the tax and the amortized dictionary
wrong: The width of the fixed-length code
The raw size of the entry
The size of the dictionary alone
why: It is the scientific number — the floor any coder with the same model could reach.
title: Two rates for everything

q: What does the fixed-length rate measure?
a: The bits of a per-channel fixed-width code with escapes for the rare large residuals, plus the tax and the dictionary
wrong: The bits of a Huffman code
The bits of the raw 8-bit values
why: It is the engineering number — what a fast GPU decoder achieves, and directly the delta size of the store.
title: Two rates for everything

q: Why does the store use the fixed-length rate for its deltas, although it is larger?
a: Every element has the same width, so any entry decodes alone and at gather speed
wrong: Because fixed-length codes are always smaller
why: Random access and GPU throughput. A stream coder must decode front to back; the miss path reads scattered single entries.
title: Two rates for everything

q: For Laplace-shaped residuals at 5–7 bits per element, how far apart are the two rates?
a: About one bit per element (15–22 % with the best width; more with a 99.5 % coverage rule)
why: A fixed width rounds up to whole bits and must cover the tail, which costs about a bit over the entropy. SplitZip’s BF16 numbers show a gap of the same size in bits (0.9–1.5).
title: Two rates for everything

q: Why does E4M3 favour solo coding?
a: Its logarithmic grid gives a bell-shaped channel an order-0 entropy of 6.47 bits at any scale, against 7.05 on a per-channel INT8 grid
wrong: Because E4M3 has more codes than INT8
Because E4M3 values are always smaller
Because E4M3 has no sign bit
why: The log grid packs codes near zero, where values are, and spends few on the big values — at the price of coarser precision for them.
title: The 8-bit grid gives and takes

q: Why can a good prediction cost bits in E4M3 index space?
a: A value and its prediction on opposite sides of zero are many grid steps apart, because the grid is dense near zero
wrong: Because E4M3 cannot store negative numbers
Because index space has fewer values
why: −3 predicted by 6 is 144 E4M3 steps but only 5 INT8 steps. Small values near a non-zero prediction produce huge residuals.
title: The 8-bit grid gives and takes

q: In E4M3 index space, below what share of variance explained is a block-mean predictor net negative?
a: About R² = 0.7
why: Our Monte Carlo (n = 400,000) reproduces the source draft — −0.81 bit at R² = 0.3, zero near 0.7, and about 0.8 bit behind INT8 above it, at any channel scale.
title: The 8-bit grid gives and takes

q: What does the per-channel “predict or not” flag do?
a: For each channel the coder stores either the raw codes or the residuals, whichever is cheaper, and spends one bit per channel saying which
wrong: It switches the whole cache between E4M3 and INT8
It turns the dictionary off for a block
why: The harness scores min(raw, residual) per channel. The flag costs one bit per channel per dictionary, almost nothing.
title: The 8-bit grid gives and takes

q: Above roughly which R² does INT8 with a per-channel scale store fewer bits in total than E4M3 (solo coding included)?
a: About 0.55
why: E4M3 starts 0.58 bit lower (6.47 against 7.05) but gains less from prediction; the curves cross near 0.55, after which INT8 stores up to 0.3 bit less.
title: The 8-bit grid gives and takes

q: Why do we expect most dictionary gains in the keys, and why keys before RoPE?
a: Keys are reported to have a few channels with very large, slowly varying values; RoPE’s position-dependent rotation smears that per-channel structure
wrong: Because keys are stored in INT8
why: Storing keys before RoPE and applying the rotation after decoding is cheap, and keeps the structure a loc dictionary can catch.
title: Where the bits would come from

q: In a model with MLA (as in the reference setting), what is different about the prior?
a: An entry is one compressed latent vector (plus a small position part), not separate keys and values — so the keys-versus-values split does not apply directly
wrong: Nothing — MLA stores keys and values separately
why: The K/V prior comes from models like the proxy (separate keys and values per head). For MLA latents it has to be measured afresh.
title: Where the bits would come from

q: If values compress no better than solo coding, and keys save 1 bit per element over a 7.24-bit fixed-length solo rate, what is the entry’s delta ratio?
a: About 0.84
why: Keys 6.24 bits, values 7.24 bits, average 6.74 bits per element: ρ ≈ 6.74/8 = 0.84. That is the draft’s “ρ capped near 0.85”.
title: Where the bits would come from

q: 16 key channels out of a 640-element entry each save 3 bits. What does that add up to per element of the entry?
a: About 0.075 bit
why: 16 × 3 = 48 bits per entry, over 640 elements. Outlier channels compress well but are few bytes.
title: Where the bits would come from

q: Which scope’s dictionary is fit once, offline, on a calibration corpus and shared by every request?
a: Global scope (the Globe)
wrong: None — every dictionary belongs to one request
why: A global dictionary is like the almanac — written once for everyone. It costs nothing at serving time and captures only what all texts have in common.
title: Dictionary scope: global, request, block

q: Request scope is the same thing as block scope with which block size?
a: b=L — one block covering the whole request
wrong: b=1 — one token per block
b=B — one block per hot cache
b=k — one block per selection
why: The scopes are nested. Stretch a block until it covers the whole request and its dictionary becomes the request’s dictionary.
title: Dictionary scope: global, request, block

q: In the reference setting, what does a request-scope dictionary of weight w=256 cost on the link?
a: About 12.8 MB, once, when the request is admitted
wrong: About 12.8 MB at every decode step
Nothing — it lives in host memory
why: weNL​=256×640 B×78≈12.8 MB — about one step’s worth of miss traffic, paid once per request.
title: Dictionary scope: global, request, block

q: Block scope, every dictionary kept on the GPU, L=100K, b=4096, w=256. How much GPU memory do the dictionaries take per layer?
a: 25 × 256 = 6400 entries’ worth — more than the 4096-slot hot cache itself
wrong: Nothing — dictionaries are stored in host memory
why: There are ⌈100K/4096⌉ = 25 blocks, each with its own 256-entry dictionary. Heavy per-block dictionaries cannot all stay resident.
title: Dictionary scope: global, request, block

q: What does the block-scope gain gblk​ measure?
a: Bits per element saved by per-block dictionaries over a per-request one of the same type
wrong: Bits saved by a global dictionary over no dictionary
The hit-rate gain of a bigger hot cache
The difference between two dictionary types at the same scope
why: It is fallen-apple similarity at block scale, in bits — the number the whole proposal bets on.
title: Dictionary scope: global, request, block

q: A dictionary of weight w=256 is shared by a block of b=4096 entries. What does it cost per element?
a: 0.5 bit
why: 8w/b=8×256/4096=0.5 bit per element — a large share of what a block dictionary can hope to save.
title: The amortization rule

q: Why do neither the entry size e nor the dimension d appear in 8w/b?
a: At 8 bits per element an entry of e bytes has d=e elements, so they cancel
wrong: Because the dictionary is stored in host memory
Because every dictionary has the same size
Because 8w/b is only an approximation for large blocks
why: The dictionary has 8we bits; the block has bd elements; with e=d the ratio is 8w/b.
title: The amortization rule

q: Which limit on the block size does the amortization rule set?
a: The smallest block a dictionary type can afford
wrong: Both the smallest and the largest
Neither: it only concerns the GPU memory
why: 8w/b falls as b grows, so it puts a floor under b. The data (how fast statistics drift) sets the ceiling.
title: The amortization rule

q: In a 100K-token request, what is “a block of 128K tokens”?
a: Not a block at all — it is request scope
wrong: The ideal block for a 256-centroid codebook
why: A block longer than the request covers the whole request, so its dictionary is the request’s dictionary.
title: The amortization rule

q: With dictionary cost capped at 0.25 bit per element, what is the smallest block a 256-centroid VQ codebook can afford?
a: About 8K tokens
why: b≥8×256/0.25=8192.
title: The amortization rule

q: Which term of Tstep​ costs link bytes even if no miss ever happens?
a: The dictionary loads, nload​NL​we
wrong: The δ-miss traffic, mkNL​efD​ρ
The raw-miss traffic, mkNL​e(1−fD​)
The hot cache, NL​eB
why: Loads are paid whenever a dictionary is brought onto the GPU, whatever the misses do. They are the price of keeping the right almanacs at hand.

q: What is wres​ for block scope with a dictionary cache of nD​ dictionaries, each of weight w?
a: nD​w entries per layer
wrong: ⌈L/b⌉w
w
why: Only the nD​ cached dictionaries sit on the GPU. Keeping all of them would cost ⌈L/b⌉w; request scope costs w.
title: The economics, written out

q: HiSparse is the special case of the cost model with which settings?
a: ρ=1, nload​=0, wres​=0
wrong: ρ=0, fD​=1
B=0, m=1
w=b

q: In the reference setting with B=4096, HiSparse serves about 109 requests per GPU. What limits it?
a: The link; GPU memory would allow about 147
wrong: GPU memory; the link would allow about 147

title: The economics, written out

q: A request-scope dictionary with w=256 and an assumed ρ=0.75 lifts the reference setting from 109 to about…
a: 138 requests per GPU, now limited by GPU memory

q: Which inputs of the what-if calculator are assumptions waiting to be measured?
a: The delta ratio ρ, the weight w, the δ-miss fraction fD​ and the load rate nload​
wrong: The context length L and the selections k
The link speed and the step time
The number of layers NL​

q: In the reference setting with B=4096, which constraint binds in every design that uses deltas?
a: GPU memory
why: Cheaper misses lift the link bound quickly. After that, the hot cache plus resident dictionaries decide how many requests fit.
title: A what-if calculator

q: With a hot cache of 4096 raw slots, what is the most lever 1 (cheaper misses) can ever give in the reference setting?
a: About 147 requests per GPU, 1.34× HiSparse
why: The hot cache alone takes 205 MB per request and 30 GB holds about 147 of them, however small the misses get.
title: A what-if calculator

q: Per-block dictionaries of weight 256, all kept on the GPU (b=4096), give about how many requests per GPU?
a: About 57 — fewer than HiSparse’s 109
why: 25 dictionaries of 256 entries per layer outweigh the hot cache itself, so memory per request more than doubles.
title: A what-if calculator

q: What does an assumed ρ=0.55 mean in bits per element?
a: About 4.4 bits — roughly 2 bits better than solo coding, which is a lot to ask
why: bpe=8ρ=4.4. Saving two bits beyond solo coding needs a dictionary that explains about 94 % of the remaining variance.
title: A what-if calculator

q: One load of a dictionary of weight w moves as many bytes over the link as…
a: w raw misses
wrong: b raw misses
why: A dictionary is we bytes; a raw miss is e bytes.
title: Two break-even conditions

q: With assumed fD​=0.85 and ρ=0.65 at B=4096, how many entries’ worth of loads per layer per step can a dictionary cache afford before it loses to HiSparse?
a: About 82 — not the 274 of the rule of thumb
why: Loads must cost less than what δ-misses save: fD​(1−ρ)mk=0.85×0.35×274≈82.
title: Two break-even conditions

q: With 4 resident dictionaries of weight 256 (same assumptions), how long must each one stay useful just to break even?
a: At least about 13 decode steps
wrong: Any time at all — loads are free
why: Break-even allows about 82/256 ≈ 0.32 loads per step per layer; 4 dictionaries replaced at that rate live about 4/0.32 ≈ 13 steps.
title: Two break-even conditions

q: At 110 requests per GPU in the reference setting, how fast must the miss-path decoder emit raw-equivalent bytes?
a: About 50 GB/s per GPU
why: 110 requests × 13.7 MB per step ÷ 30 ms ≈ 50 GB/s — exactly what the link would have carried raw.
title: Two break-even conditions

q: Why does the store want fixed-length deltas rather than an rANS-style entropy coder?
a: Fixed-length GPU decoders run at 0.5–2 TB/s, an order of magnitude above the need; entropy decoders are borderline
wrong: Entropy coders need a dictionary per element
why: SplitZip’s fixed-length decoder reaches 565 GB/s (E5M2) and 2.2 TB/s (BF16) on an H200; rANS-style decoders run at tens to a few hundred GB/s.
title: Two break-even conditions

q: Why rehearse the measurement on synthetic data before touching a real KV cache?
a: Its structure is known, so the method must recover what was planted — and find nothing where nothing was planted
wrong: Synthetic data compresses better, so the results look good
Real KV caches cannot be read from a GPU
why: A known answer turns the data itself into a test of the code. It says nothing about KV caches.
title: A synthetic dress rehearsal

q: What does the shuffle control do?
a: Permutes tokens across sequences and reruns everything; every gain that depends on neighbours must vanish
wrong: Reorders the channels of each entry
Drops a random half of the tokens
why: After shuffling, a block’s tokens are strangers to each other. A block-local gain that survives is a bug or a bias.
title: A synthetic dress rehearsal

q: In the rehearsal, at which block size is the loc rate lowest, and why?
a: At 2048 tokens — the true length of the planted blocks
wrong: At 128 tokens — smaller blocks always fit better
At 8192 tokens — the dictionary is cheapest there
It does not depend on the block size
why: Smaller blocks pay more for their dictionaries and fit noisier; larger blocks straddle two planted blocks and fit neither.
title: A synthetic dress rehearsal

q: What does the 256-centroid VQ do in the rehearsal?
a: It needs blocks of 8K just to pay for its codebook, and then is no better than loc
wrong: It beats every other type at every block size
It wins only at small blocks
why: On bell-shaped data a codebook only recovers, with a tax, what cheaper dictionaries get anyway — as VI.7’s napkin predicted.
title: A synthetic dress rehearsal

q: In the shuffled run, the KLT bound still dips below the global KLT line at small blocks. What does that reveal?
a: The bound fits its own noise there — read it only at blocks much longer than d, and against its own shuffled value
wrong: Shuffling failed to remove the structure
The data has real token-level structure
The global line was computed wrongly
why: A 64×64 covariance estimated from 128 tokens fits those very tokens. The shuffle control exposes the bias, which is exactly its job.
title: A synthetic dress rehearsal

q: Which sentence of the first draft does this Part keep coming back to?
a: “HiSparse’s high hit rate shows that this ladder is steep at the bottom rung, so a block dictionary should work.”
wrong: “A block dictionary is too heavy to keep on the GPU.”
“The KV cache cannot be compressed losslessly.”
why: It sounds like measurement → conclusion → design, and every step of it needs a correction (VII.2, VII.3, VII.6).
title: The first draft, and why corrections are a gift

q: How many items does “What Dima missed” collect, and in which groups?
a: Sixteen — 7 corrections, 5 fields and tools, 4 design changes
why: Corrections are VII.2–VII.8, fields and tools VII.9–VII.13, design changes VII.14–VII.17.
title: The first draft, and why corrections are a gift

q: Why does this site call the corrections a gift?
a: Each one sharpened a question and changed the plan before any GPU time was spent
wrong: They prove that the idea does not work
They are what reviewers ask for
why: A wrong claim found on paper costs an afternoon. Found after a weekend of measuring the wrong thing, it costs the weekend.
title: The first draft, and why corrections are a gift

q: Did any of the seven corrections overturn the direction of the idea?
a: No — each changes how the idea is measured or built, not where it points
why: Dictionaries plus deltas on the miss path survive every item. What changes is the evidence, the default dictionary, the number format and the codec’s shape.
title: The first draft, and why corrections are a gift

q: HiSparse’s LRU hot cache hits about 87 % of selections at B = 2k. What does that number tell you about?
a: Which entries the indexer keeps selecting from step to step
wrong: How alike neighbouring entries’ bytes are
How many bits a block dictionary would save
How compressible the KV history is
why: A hit means “selected again soon”. It compares one step’s query with the next step’s query; it never compares one stored entry with another.
title: Two localities were merged

q: In the toy, the stored bytes are shuffled across positions while the selections stay the same. What happens?
a: The hit rate stays at 89 %; the bits saved by a neighbour fall from 1.61 to about 0
wrong: The hit rate falls; the bits stay at 1.61
why: Selections depend on the indexer’s query, not on the bytes. Shuffling destroys neighbour similarity but leaves every selection where it was.
title: Two localities were merged

q: Which corner of the 2 × 2 does the first leak toy of IV.13 occupy?
a: Slow query, unrelated bytes — HiSparse-like hits, zero compression
why: IV.13 draws keys independently, so no neighbour helps, and drifts the query slowly, so the cache hits anyway.
title: Two localities were merged

q: Which question about “which entries” does the block design genuinely need answered?
a: Whether misses pile into a few heavy blocks that stay in use for many steps
wrong: Whether the LRU hit rate is above 80 %
Whether neighbouring entries have similar bytes
Whether the indexer is DSA or NSA
why: Block dictionaries are cheap to keep on the GPU only if misses concentrate in a few long-lived blocks (IV.10, question Q3).
title: Two localities were merged

q: How does the plan test fallen-apple similarity directly?
a: Bits per element of an entry given a neighbour, at 8 bits, with a shuffle control
wrong: By replaying HiSparse’s trace and reading the hit rate
By measuring cosine similarity of neighbouring keys
why: The quantity is about bytes, so it is measured on bytes, in bits, and must vanish when tokens are shuffled.
title: Two localities were merged

q: Knowing the dictionary D makes an entry E more predictable. What happens to I(E; D) and to H(E | D)?
a: I(E; D) goes up and H(E | D) goes down
wrong: I(E; D) goes down and H(E | D) goes up
why: Mutual information is the bits saved, I=H(E)−H(E∣D). More predictable means fewer bits still to pay, so more bits saved.
title: Predictability is mutual information, not its reverse

q: In the cat-thread toy at strength 0.5, how many bits does knowing the breed save, on average?
why: Nothing known costs 2 bits; knowing the breed leaves 1.55; the difference, 0.45 bits, is I(X;breed). The thread alone saves 0.19.
title: Predictability is mutual information, not its reverse

q: A rare value d turns up in a Maine Coon block. With the breed known, its code gets…
a: Longer — 3 bits instead of 2
why: Conditioning never hurts on average, but a single unusual outcome can cost more once the context says it is unusual.
title: Predictability is mutual information, not its reverse

q: The ladder H(E) ≥ H(E | thread) ≥ H(E | block) is a theorem. Why can a measured scope gain still come out negative?
a: Real side information costs bits, and a dictionary fit on finite data is not the true distribution
wrong: Because the theorem only holds for Gaussian data
It cannot: measured gains are always positive
why: The theorem assumes free, perfect side information. A real dictionary has a price (8w/b) and a fitted model pays cross-entropy, not entropy.
title: Predictability is mutual information, not its reverse

q: HiSparse’s trace has 100,384 tokens. What is a “128K-token block” of it?
a: The whole request — one block, which is the request scope
wrong: A block with 31K tokens of padding that compresses for free
why: 131,072 > 100,384, so the “block” holds every token of the request. That is scope request, not scope block.
title: The block is a knob, not a property

q: How many blocks of b = 2048 tokens does a 100,384-token request have?
a: 50 — the last one holds 32 tokens
why: The count is ⌈t / b⌉ = 50. The first draft’s “t % b” (here 32) is the size of the last, partial block, not the number of blocks.
title: The block is a knob, not a property

q: In the toy with a 2K-token drift length, which dictionary weight never pays at any block size?
a: w = 256 (a codebook)
wrong: None — every dictionary pays at a large enough block
why: At small blocks its cost 8w/b is huge; by the time b is large enough to amortize it, the blocks have outgrown the drift and the gain is gone.
