title: The block is a knob, not a property

q: In the toy, what moves the best block size?
a: Both the data’s drift length and the dictionary’s weight
wrong: Neither — the best block is always 64K tokens
why: Gain is set by the data (it fades as blocks outgrow the drift); cost 8w/b is set by the dictionary. The best b is where they balance — an output of the analysis.
title: The block is a knob, not a property

q: How does the plan choose the block size?
a: It sweeps several sizes and reads b off the measured distance curve, capped by 8w/b
wrong: It fixes b = 128K tokens as in the first draft
It uses the hot-cache size B as the block size
It picks the largest block that fits in HBM
why: The hypothesis is a curve over token distance; the block size is a design knob tuned to it.
title: The block is a knob, not a property

q: In lossless terms, what is “VQ, then entropy-code the error”?
a: Predictive coding with the nearest centroid as the prediction, plus the centroid’s index as per-entry side information
wrong: A rotation of the data to its KLT axes
LZ matching against a codebook of byte strings
why: The centroid is the guess, the exact residual is stored, and the index — log₂ C bits per entry — is the tax.
title: "VQ, then entropy-code the error" cannot beat a rotation on Gaussian data

q: On the smooth-hill toy (correlated bell), what is the best the codebook nets, and what does the rotation get?
a: About 0.29 bit per element (C = 4) against 0.59 for the rotation
why: The codebook narrows the leftover by 1.30 bits but pays 1.01 in index and codebook tax. The rotation pays nothing per entry.
title: "VQ, then entropy-code the error" cannot beat a rotation on Gaussian data

q: On the 16-clumps toy, why does the rotation get almost nothing?
a: The channels are already uncorrelated, so there is no better pair of axes to turn to
wrong: Because rotations only work in high dimension
Because the clumps make the variance infinite
Because the rotation pays an index tax
why: A rotation exploits correlation. Clumps scattered without a preferred direction have none; a codebook exploits the clumps themselves.
title: "VQ, then entropy-code the error" cannot beat a rotation on Gaussian data

q: In a 640-element entry, the index of a 4-centroid codebook costs only 0.003 bits per element. Why does VQ still not win on bell-shaped data?
a: On a bell, the narrowing beyond the rotation shrinks by the same factor as the tax
wrong: Because the index must be stored in BF16
It does win in high dimension
why: Rate–distortion: R bits per vector buy at most R/d bits per element of narrowing beyond the transform — exactly the tax.
title: "VQ, then entropy-code the error" cannot beat a rotation on Gaussian data

q: What does the plan do with VQ after this correction?
a: Starts with light dictionaries and measures VQ as one rung, to find out whether KV entries clump
wrong: Uses VQ as the default dictionary
Replaces the rotation with product quantization
why: Whether KV clumps (by token type, template position, sink tokens) is an empirical question the measurement answers directly.
title: "VQ, then entropy-code the error" cannot beat a rotation on Gaussian data

q: Every element of an entry is correlated 0.95 with the same element of its neighbour. How many bits per element does the neighbour save, at most (bell-shaped data)?
a: About 1.68 bits — still about 4.8 of 6.47 bits to pay
why: The neighbour explains 0.952=90.25% of the variance; 21​log2​0.09751​≈1.68 bits.
title: Lossless is a game of variance explained

q: How much of the remaining variance must a predictor explain to save 2 bits per element?
why: Each bit halves the standard deviation, which removes three quarters of the variance left. Two bits leave 1/16, so 15/16 must be explained.
title: Lossless is a game of variance explained

q: If 30 % of an entry’s variance is pure noise, what is the most any dictionary can save per element?
a: About 0.87 bit
why: At best the dictionary explains the other 70 %: 21​log2​0.31​≈0.87 bit, out of 6.47.
title: Lossless is a game of variance explained

q: Sixteen channels, average R² = 30 %. Spread evenly they save 0.26 bit per element. Two channels at 99 %, the rest at 20 %, save…
a: 0.56 bit — more than twice as much
wrong: 3.3 bits — the two giants dominate everything
why: The exchange rate is gentle at low R² and steep near 100 %, so concentrated predictability buys more bits than the same amount spread thin.
title: Lossless is a game of variance explained

q: What does the plan measure because of the escape hatch?
a: R² and bits saved for every channel, keys and values separately, not only the average
wrong: Only the average R² over the whole entry
why: A few nearly predictable channels can carry most of the gain; an average hides them.
title: Lossless is a game of variance explained

q: For a bell-shaped channel stored in BF16 with no predictor, what do sign, exponent and mantissa cost?
a: About 1.0 + 2.5 + 7.0 ≈ 10.5 bits, so at most about 1.5× smaller
why: The exponent is predictable, the mantissa is not. Published lossless coders get 1.3–1.5× on BF16 for this reason.
title: The mantissa is noise, and the 8-bit grid is not neutral

q: A prediction explains 90 % of a channel’s variance. How many of the 16 BF16 bits are still close to coin flips?
a: 8 of 16 — the 7 mantissa bits and the lowest exponent bit
wrong: None — 90 % is a very good prediction
why: The residual’s spread is about a third of the value’s, far wider than the mantissa’s step, so every mantissa bit stays unknown.
title: The mantissa is noise, and the 8-bit grid is not neutral

q: A value 0.40 is predicted as −0.10. How far apart are they on the E4M3 grid and on the INT8 grid (scale 4/127)?
a: 74 steps on E4M3, 16 steps on INT8
why: E4M3’s grid is dense near zero, so a residual that crosses zero spans many grid points. INT8’s grid is even.
title: The mantissa is noise, and the 8-bit grid is not neutral

q: What does the E4M3 grid do to prediction and to solo coding?
a: It helps solo coding (6.47 vs 7.04 bits) and hurts prediction in index space
wrong: It hurts solo coding and helps prediction
why: A logarithmic grid makes a bell-shaped channel cheap on its own, but turns small differences near zero into many steps.
title: The mantissa is noise, and the 8-bit grid is not neutral

q: What does the plan do about the grid?
a: Scores both E4M3 and INT8 with a scale, and gives every channel a one-bit “predict or not” flag
wrong: Uses E4M3 only and ignores the effect
why: Both are 8-bit storage formats an inference system may choose; the flag stops prediction from making a channel worse.
title: The mantissa is noise, and the 8-bit grid is not neutral

q: What does the miss path read per layer per decode step in the reference setting (B = 4096)?
a: About 274 scattered entries of 640 bytes, each needed on its own
wrong: About 274 entries, read front to back from position 0
why: 13.4 % of 2048 selections miss, at arbitrary positions among 100K, and each must be rebuilt without its neighbours.
title: The access pattern decides the codec's shape

q: The history is stream-coded in chunks of 64 entries. Roughly how many bytes does one request move per layer and step on the miss path?
a: About 7.2 MB, against 140 KB for fixed-length deltas
why: About 251 chunks are touched, and each must be read and decoded whole to reach one entry.
title: The access pattern decides the codec's shape

q: Stream coding is 0.70 of raw and fixed-length 0.80. From what chunk size does the stream lose on bytes moved?
a: Already at 2 entries per chunk
why: Two entries at 0.70 each cost 1.40 entries’ worth to deliver one; a fixed-length delta costs 0.80.
title: The access pattern decides the codec's shape

q: What exactly does random access forbid?
a: Coder state shared between entries
why: A per-entry entropy code is allowed; it needs an offset table and a second read. Fixed-length deltas are preferred for simple addressing and fast decoding.
title: The access pattern decides the codec's shape

q: In the toy, why is a per-entry variable-length code (one entry per chunk) not the default even though it moves fewer bytes?
a: It needs a per-entry offset and a second dependent read, and decodes each entry serially
wrong: Because it moves more bytes than raw entries
Because it needs the whole block decoded
why: Fixed-length deltas give address = base + offset in one read and a decode that is a gather and an add. The 10–15 % gap between the two rates is the price of random access.
title: The access pattern decides the codec's shape

q: What do FLAC, PNG and JPEG-LS have in common with kv-blockdiff?
a: Each predicts a value from things the decoder already has, stores the exact integer residual, and codes that residual with a simple code
wrong: Each ships a trained dictionary of byte strings, like zstd
Each throws away low-order bits it judges unimportant
Each describes vectors by the nearest centroid of a codebook
why: They are all lossless predictive coders (DPCM). Only what is predicted from what changes — samples, pixels, or a block’s dictionary.
title: The real home of the problem: predictive coding with side information

q: FLAC’s order-1 predictor guesses “the same as the last sample”. By how much does it multiply the variance of white noise in the residual?
a: By 2
why: The residual is the difference of two noisy samples, and the variances of independent noises add. Order 2 multiplies by 6, order 3 by 20. The same arithmetic makes the sib dictionary’s noise double.
title: The real home of the problem: predictive coding with side information

q: What did Slepian and Wolf (1973) show?
a: Lossless coding can reach H(X | Y) even when only the decoder knows Y
wrong: Side information helps only when both ends have it
Side information always halves the rate
Lossless coding with side information needs a trained dictionary
why: The surprise is that the encoder need not see Y. It only has to send which “bin” X falls in; the decoder picks the bin member that fits Y. Practical versions need long blocks.
title: The real home of the problem: predictive coding with side information

q: In kv-blockdiff, where is the side information?
a: At both ends — the encoder sees the whole block offline, and the GPU holds the block’s dictionary when it decodes
wrong: At the decoder only, as in Slepian–Wolf
Nowhere; each entry is coded alone
why: That is the easy, classical case; the rate is H(E | D). The catch is residency — a δ-miss exists only if the dictionary really is on the GPU.
title: The real home of the problem: predictive coding with side information

q: Why does naming the “real home” of the problem change the plan?
a: It imports finished tools and bounds — residual codes, context modelling, lifting, coding-gain bounds — instead of reinventing them
wrong: It makes the KV papers irrelevant
It proves that the idea works
It replaces the need for measurements
why: Lossless audio and image coding already solved most engineering sub-problems of this shape; what they cannot supply is the KV statistics.
title: The real home of the problem: predictive coding with side information

q: Why is “rotate in floating point, then round to integers” not lossless?
a: Rounding can send two different inputs to the same integer point, and then no decoder can tell which one it was
wrong: Because floating-point rotations are not exact
Because a rotation changes the variance of the data
Because integers cannot be rotated at all
why: In the figure, 12 of the 81 points vanish into collisions at 45°. A many-to-one step cannot be undone.
title: Lifting: how a rotation becomes lossless

q: Why can the shear x1​←x1​−round(ax2​), with a fixed slope a, be undone exactly?
a: It leaves x2​ unchanged, so the decoder can recompute the very same rounded shift and add it back
wrong: Because rounding errors cancel on average
Because the slope is always an integer
Because the decoder stores the rounding error separately
why: The rounded amount depends only on the coordinate that did not move. Inverse — same step with the opposite sign.
title: Lifting: how a rotation becomes lossless

q: How many integer shears does a 2-D rotation need?
a: Three — shear the first coordinate, then the second, then the first again
wrong: As many as the angle in degrees
why: Rotation by θ = shear by −tan(θ/2), then by sin θ, then by −tan(θ/2) again.
title: Lifting: how a rotation becomes lossless

q: Each lifting step is an instance of which running idea?
a: Predict, then store only the surprise — predict one coordinate from the other and keep the exact residual
wrong: Which entries versus what is inside them
why: x1​−round(ax2​) is literally “the value minus its prediction from the other coordinate”.
title: Lifting: how a rotation becomes lossless

q: Why does wave 1 not implement a lossless KLT?
a: It computes the KLT’s bound from the spectrum first; lifting is built only if that bound beats the light dictionaries by enough
wrong: Because lifting cannot be used on GPUs
Because a KLT is always lossy
Because the KLT has already been ruled out
why: A full lossless rotation is heavy (about d² multiply-adds per entry, a 2d-entry dictionary). The bound decides whether that cost can pay.
title: Lifting: how a rotation becomes lossless

q: What does context modelling do with a prediction?
a: It uses the prediction to choose the probability table for the value, instead of subtracting it
wrong: It subtracts the prediction and codes the difference
It stores the prediction next to the value
It discards values that differ from the prediction
why: The cost of a value becomes −log₂ p(x | x̂), averaging H(X | X̂), which is never more than H(X).
title: Context modelling never loses

q: On the E4M3 grid, a value of −0.5 is predicted as +0.5. How many grid steps apart are they?
why: The grid is densest near zero, so this small miss crosses dozens of codes. A miss of the same size between 4.5 and 5.5 is only 2 steps.
title: Context modelling never loses

q: In the exact toy, below roughly which share of variance explained is subtraction in E4M3 index space worse than no prediction at all?
a: About 0.70
why: With one table for all residuals, the wide residuals of predictions near zero spoil the narrow ones. Context modelling stays below the no-prediction line at every R².
title: Context modelling never loses

q: Why does subtraction work as well as context modelling on INT8?
a: On a uniform grid the surprise has the same shape wherever the prediction lands, so one residual table fits every context
wrong: Because INT8 has fewer codes than E4M3
Because INT8 values are never near zero
why: Subtraction silently assumes shift-invariance. A uniform grid has it; a logarithmic grid does not.
title: Context modelling never loses

q: Why can context modelling not replace the fixed-length miss path?
a: Its code lengths depend on the context’s table, so it needs an entropy coder; it serves the entropy-rate column
wrong: Because it needs a dictionary of hundreds of entries
Because it cannot use the block’s prediction
why: On E4M3, contexts near zero genuinely need wide codes; the gain lives in variable-length coding.
title: Context modelling never loses

q: Why does one pass over a trace give LRU’s misses at every cache size?
a: An LRU cache of B slots always holds exactly the top B items of the recency stack, so each request’s depth in that stack says at once for which sizes it hits
wrong: Because the miss rate is the same at every size
Because the trace is replayed once per size in parallel
why: This nesting (a smaller cache’s contents sit inside a larger one’s) is Mattson’s inclusion property. Misses at size B = requests with stack distance at least B.
title: The stack-distance curve behind every cache number

q: On the string 1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5, FIFO misses 9 times with 3 slots. With 4 slots it misses…
a: 10 times — more, with a bigger cache (Bélády’s anomaly)
why: FIFO’s contents at 3 slots are not a subset of its contents at 4, so it has no single stack curve. LRU and Bélády’s policy do.
title: The stack-distance curve behind every cache number

q: If the miss rate follows m(B)∝B−1.08, doubling the hot cache multiplies the misses by about…
why: 2−1.08≈0.47. HiSparse’s points: 30 % at 2048, 13.4 % at 4096, 6.7 % at 8192.
title: The stack-distance curve behind every cache number

q: With the power law above, cheaper slots (lever 2) plus cheaper misses (lever 1) cut miss traffic by about what factor for ρ = 0.65?
why: The cache grows by 1/ρ at equal memory, so misses fall by ρ^1.08; each miss is ρ smaller. Traffic ∝ ρ^2.08 = 0.41.
title: The stack-distance curve behind every cache number

q: What does wave 2 measure instead of extrapolating HiSparse’s three points?
a: The whole stack-distance histogram of the proxy trace, in one pass — every cache size, the victim tier and the dictionary cache read off directly
wrong: Only the miss rate at B = 4096
The Bélády miss rate at every size
The hit rate of the indexer
why: One pass gives the full curve; the same pass over block ids gives the dictionary cache’s curve.
title: The stack-distance curve behind every cache number

q: What is the KLT gain of a perfectly flat spectrum (all eigenvalues equal)?
a: Zero — AM equals GM, so rotating buys nothing
wrong: It depends on the number of dimensions
why: The gain is ½ log₂(AM/GM), and for equal eigenvalues AM = GM. Rotation helps only when the spread is uneven.
title: Bounds before building

q: 64 directions, 8 with variance 10 and 56 with variance 1. About how many bits per element can a rotation save?
a: About 0.34
why: AM = 136/64 = 2.13, GM = 10^(8/64) = 1.33; ½ log₂(1.59) = 0.34. “Low-rank-ish” is not enough; the spectrum must be sharply spiky.
title: Bounds before building

q: A codebook of 256 centroids for 64-element vectors pays what index tax per element?
why: log₂ 256 = 8 bits per vector, spread over 64 elements. On Gaussian data that is also the most the centroid can save beyond a rotation.
title: Bounds before building

q: When can vector quantization beat the rate–distortion bound computed for Gaussian data?
a: When the data is genuinely clustered, which a Gaussian model cannot describe
wrong: When the codebook is large enough
why: The bound is a statement about Gaussian data. In the old draft’s Monte Carlo, 32 real clusters let VQ net +1.5 bits where a rotation got +0.68.
title: Bounds before building

q: What does the one-hour experiment 1a compute?
a: Grid-free bounds from the float data — the distance curve’s R² in bits, the location gain and the KLT gain — with a shuffle control
wrong: The exact lossless rates on E4M3 codes
Requests per GPU from a trace replay
A trained VQ codebook per block
why: Bounds first; the exact ladder (1b) follows either way, because the 8-bit grid can take back part of what floats promise.
title: Bounds before building

q: About how much does the loc dictionary weigh, in entries’ worth?
a: About 2 — one location and one scale per channel
why: An entry has one 8-bit number per channel; a location and a scale per channel are about two entries’ worth.
title: Light dictionaries first

q: In the reference setting with blocks of 2,048 tokens, what does keeping a loc dictionary for every block cost, per layer?
a: About 98 entries’ worth — 2.4 % of a 4,096-slot hot cache
wrong: About 4,096 entries’ worth — as much as the hot cache
why: 100,000 / 2,048 ≈ 49 blocks × w = 2 ≈ 98. Per request, across 78 layers, that is about 4.9 MB against a 205 MB hot cache.
title: Light dictionaries first

q: If every block’s dictionary is resident, what are the δ-miss fraction and the dictionary-load rate?
a: Every miss is a δ-miss (fD​=1), and no dictionaries are loaded during decoding (nload​=0)
wrong: Half the misses are δ-misses, with one load per step
It depends on the residency policy
None — light dictionaries cannot serve misses
why: Every miss finds its dictionary on the GPU; there is no residency policy to tune and no dictionary traffic.
title: Light dictionaries first

q: With ρ = 0.75 assumed, blocks of 2,048 and every dictionary resident, which type gains on HiSparse’s 109 requests per GPU?
a: loc (about 143, 1.31×); a rank-16 basis already loses a little (106)
wrong: None — residency always costs too much
why: The light dictionary costs 2.4 % of the hot cache; the rank-16 basis costs 38 %, and the codebook three times the hot cache.
title: Light dictionaries first

q: When does framework C (where misses land) become necessary?
a: Only if wave 1 shows that heavy dictionaries are needed — that is, if the data is clustered
wrong: Only for values, never for keys
why: With light dictionaries all resident, f_D = 1 by construction; residency matters only for dictionaries too heavy to keep everywhere.
title: Light dictionaries first

q: A pair of key channels sits near the same point token after token. What does RoPE do to it?
a: It rotates the pair by an angle that grows with position, smearing the tight cluster into an arc or a whole ring
wrong: It adds random noise to every channel
It shrinks the pair toward zero
why: RoPE rotates each pair of key channels by position × that pair’s frequency. A per-channel location (loc) can no longer predict a value that keeps turning.
title: Keys before RoPE; keys and values as separate problems

q: Within one block, which RoPE pairs does a block-scope loc dictionary still handle well?
a: The slow pairs, whose angle changes by much less than a radian across the block
wrong: The fast pairs, which turn once every few tokens
why: A slowly turning pair traces a short arc inside a block, close to a point. A fast pair traces whole circles.
title: Keys before RoPE; keys and values as separate problems

q: Why store keys before RoPE?
a: Before the spin the structured channels are nearly constant and cheap to predict; the decoder rebuilds the pre-RoPE key exactly and applies the rotation for the known position
wrong: Because attention never uses rotated keys
Because pre-RoPE keys are smaller in bytes
why: The rotation after decoding is a cheap element-wise operation. KVQuant also quantizes keys before RoPE.
title: Keys before RoPE; keys and values as separate problems

q: Values stay at their fixed-length solo rate (7 bits per element) and keys reach 6.6 bits. What is the entry’s delta ratio?
a: About 0.85
why: The entry’s ρ is the byte-weighted mean of its halves: (6.6 + 7) / 16 = 0.85. Even free keys would leave ρ = 7/16.
title: Keys before RoPE; keys and values as separate problems

q: If values show nothing beyond solo coding, how should they be stored?
a: With a global, context-free code — no dictionary, no residency — while dictionaries are spent on keys only
wrong: With per-block dictionaries anyway, to be safe
why: A dictionary that saves nothing still costs weight and residency. Solo coding is free at serving time.
title: Keys before RoPE; keys and values as separate problems

q: What does the victim tier hold?
a: The deltas of entries recently evicted from the raw hot cache, whose block dictionaries are on the GPU
wrong: Raw copies of the most-used entries
Entries the indexer has not selected yet
why: A delta is ρe bytes instead of e, so the tier keeps many more evicted entries within reach for the same memory.
title: A victim tier of deltas

q: A hot cache of B raw slots plus a victim tier of BV​ deltas reaches how many entries without the link, at what GPU-memory cost?
a: B+BV​ entries, for about B+ρBV​ slots’ worth of memory (plus the dictionaries)
wrong: B entries, for B+BV​ slots
BV​ entries, for ρB slots
B+BV​ entries, for B+BV​ slots
why: Each victim-tier slot holds a delta of ρe bytes; the raw slots are unchanged.
title: A victim tier of deltas

q: Why can the victim tier’s value be read off the reuse-distance curve?
a: Under LRU, an entry sits in the victim tier exactly when its stack distance is between B and B+BV​, so the extra hits are m(B)−m(B+BV​)
wrong: Because the victim tier never misses
Because deltas are always smaller than half an entry
It cannot; it must be simulated with a GPU kernel
why: LRU is a stack algorithm; the tier is just the next BV​ rows of the recency stack.
title: A victim tier of deltas

q: Where does the victim tier’s decoding run, compared with the full lever 2?
a: At promotion time, outside the attention kernel — the full lever 2 must decode inside the attention gather
wrong: Inside the attention gather, like lever 2
Nowhere — entries in the tier are used as deltas
why: That is why it needs only the lever-1 decoder, run on promotions, instead of a fused kernel at ~370 GB/s.
title: A victim tier of deltas

q: What does wave 2 measure so the victim tier can be priced without extrapolation?
a: The full reuse-distance distribution of the proxy trace
wrong: Only the hit rate at B = 4096
The size of the deltas of evicted entries
why: With the whole distribution, m(B+BV​) is a look-up for every B and BV​.
title: A victim tier of deltas

q: Why was the Michelson–Morley null result convincing?
a: Their instrument could clearly have seen the expected effect — they expected 0.4 of a fringe and saw less than a twentieth of that
wrong: Because they repeated it a thousand times
Because the result agreed with theory
why: A null result means something only when the instrument was sensitive enough to see what the hypothesis predicts.
title: A measurement is a result

q: Which control shows that the harness could have seen fallen-apple similarity if it were there?
a: The synthetic dress rehearsal — data with planted block structure, which the method must recover
why: The rehearsal measures sensitivity (no false negatives); the shuffle control guards against false positives.
title: A measurement is a result

q: In the decision table, request-scope gain 0.5 bit and block-scope gain 0.3 bit fall where?
a: In a hole — the sum is 0.8 ≥ 0.75, but the block gain is between 0.15 and 0.4, a case the table does not name
why: The old table covers g_blk ≥ 0.4 and g_blk < 0.15 for sums above 0.75, not the band between. The plan fills it: run wave 2 with both scopes and let the trace replay decide (IX.9).
title: A measurement is a result

q: If wave 1 is negative, what does the field get?
a: A shuffle-controlled measurement that 8-bit KV has little conditional structure, and a pointer to context-free miss-path coding (about 1.1–1.3× for free)
wrong: A proof that the KV cache cannot be compressed at all
why: Nobody has published that number at 8 bits; a negative redirects effort toward solo coding on the miss path.
title: A measurement is a result

q: Which of these is an experiment-framework question rather than a big-picture question?
a: For Δ = 1, 2, 4 … 32K tokens, how many bits per element does a neighbour at distance Δ save, charged by one fixed rule?
wrong: What is KV’s fallen-apple similarity like?
Can a dictionary + delta store beat raw storage?
why: It names what is varied (Δ), what is measured (bits saved) and how it is charged. The other three are open-ended — the reasons the project exists.
title: Two kinds of questions

q: What must a framework question state before any data is taken?
a: Its possible outcomes, what each would mean, and what we would do next in each case
wrong: The answer it expects to get
Which model the paper will use
Only the hardware it runs on
why: Writing the outcome shapes down first stops every curve from being read as “promising” after the fact.
title: Two kinds of questions

q: Which big-picture question is the existence question, without which the other two do not matter?
a: Q1 — what is KV’s fallen-apple similarity like, in bits?
wrong: Q2 — can a dictionary + delta store beat raw storage?
Q3 — do misses concentrate in few blocks?
why: If entries are not cheaper to code given their neighbours, there is nothing for a dictionary to store and nothing for residency to protect.
title: Two kinds of questions

q: Which framework answers Q3, the residency question?
a: C — where misses land (replaying the indexer’s selections)
wrong: None: Q3 cannot be measured before a kernel exists
why: Q3 is about which entries are selected and how they group into blocks; replaying selection traces measures that directly.
title: Two kinds of questions

q: A clean “no” on Q3 would mean…
a: Use one dictionary per request, or light dictionaries kept resident for every block, instead of a cache of block dictionaries
wrong: HiSparse’s published hit rates are wrong
why: Every negative answer is informative. A “no” on Q3 changes the design, not the existence of the gain.
title: Two kinds of questions

q: In one sentence, what does Q1 ask?
a: How many bits per element a neighbouring entry saves when coding an entry exactly, and how that changes with their token distance Δ
wrong: How often the indexer re-selects the same entries
How much accuracy a model loses when its KV is quantized to 2 bits
Whether cosine similarity between keys is high
why: Q1 is about the bytes inside entries, measured in bits; re-selection is the Lucky Louis property, and accuracy loss is a lossy question.
title: Q1: what is KV's fallen-apple similarity like?

q: Why is HiSparse’s high hit rate not evidence for a “yes” on Q1?
a: It shows that the indexer’s query moves slowly (which entries are wanted), not that the stored entries resemble each other
wrong: Because HiSparse uses BF16, not 8 bits
Because HiSparse measured only one model
Because hit rates are measured in percent, not bits
why: A toy with keys that cannot be compressed by a single bit already gives HiSparse-like hit rates (IV.13). Which-versus-what.
title: Q1: what is KV's fallen-apple similarity like?

q: The distance curve comes out flat but clearly above zero at every Δ. What does that mean?
a: Structure shared across the whole request, not local — per-request dictionaries, not block ones
wrong: A bug, because the shuffle control must be flat too
why: A local effect would fade with distance. A flat positive curve says that far neighbours help as much as near ones.
title: Q1: what is KV's fallen-apple similarity like?

q: In the wave-1 decision rule, how much must the two scope gains add up to, at least, for a clear “yes”?
a: 0.75 bit per element, with at least 0.4 bit from the block rung
wrong: 2 bits per element from the block rung alone
why: Total ≥ 0.75 and gblk​ ≥ 0.4 reads as block-scale fallen-apple similarity; below 0.25 in total reads as “no”.
title: Q1: what is KV's fallen-apple similarity like?

q: Which lever’s payoff does Q1 set most directly?
a: Lever 1 — a δ-miss moves ρe bytes, and Q1 decides how small ρ can be
wrong: Neither — Q1 is only about residency
why: The delta ratio ρ is bits per element over 8; the bits come from the conditional structure Q1 measures.
title: Q1: what is KV's fallen-apple similarity like?

q: Why is “beat raw storage” too easy a bar for Q2?
a: Solo coding already beats raw by about 1.1–1.3× with no dictionary at all
wrong: Because raw storage is already compressed by HiSparse
Because no lossless coder can beat raw 8-bit storage
why: A global, context-free code per channel (solo) reaches ρ ≈ 0.78 ideally, ≈ 0.88 with a fixed-length code. Gains are counted from there.
title: Q2: can a dictionary + delta store beat raw storage?

q: Which of these is NOT one of the hurdles a dictionary coder must clear on the miss path?
a: It must be trained on the same request it will serve
wrong: Each entry must decode alone, given only its block’s dictionary
It must beat solo coding after paying for its dictionary
It must survive the 8-bit grid and a fixed-length format
why: Where a dictionary is fit (its scope) is a design choice, not a hurdle. Random access, the solo bar, the dictionary’s cost and the format are hurdles.
title: Q2: can a dictionary + delta store beat raw storage?

q: The best coders reach low ρ only with heavy dictionaries (thousands of centroids). What does Q2 then hand over to?
a: Q3 — whether heavy dictionaries can stay resident cheaply
why: Heavy dictionaries cost many entries’ worth to load and to keep on the GPU; whether that is affordable depends on where misses land.
title: Q2: can a dictionary + delta store beat raw storage?

q: A dictionary coder saves 0.6 bit per element over solo with an ideal coder. Roughly what is its ρ?
a: About 0.7
title: Q2: can a dictionary + delta store beat raw storage?

q: Misses spread evenly over 25 blocks, and the GPU keeps 4 block dictionaries. Roughly what is the δ-miss fraction f_D?
a: About 16 %
wrong: 100 %, because every miss has a dictionary somewhere
why: Only misses that land in one of the 4 resident blocks are δ-misses: 4 / 25 = 0.16.
title: Q3: do misses concentrate in few, long-lived blocks?

q: Why must heavy blocks also be long-lived, not just heavy?
a: Every time the set of heavy blocks changes, new dictionaries must be loaded, and each load costs w entries’ worth on the link
wrong: Because dictionaries expire after a fixed time
Because the hot cache evicts blocks, not entries
Because the indexer only selects from old blocks
why: With w = 256, a single load per step costs about as much as all 274 misses of that step. Loads must be rare: n_load · w ≪ 274.
title: Q3: do misses concentrate in few, long-lived blocks?

q: Trace replay shows f_D ≥ 0.8 with 8 or fewer resident dictionaries and under 0.1 loads per step. What does that mean?
a: Heavy block dictionaries are affordable
wrong: The hot cache is too small
why: Misses concentrate and blocks stay heavy, so even heavy dictionaries can stay on the GPU. Whether they help is Q1 and Q2’s business.
title: Q3: do misses concentrate in few, long-lived blocks?

q: For which dictionaries does Q3 not matter at all?
a: Light ones (weight w ≈ 2), because they can be resident for every block at once
wrong: Heavy codebooks with thousands of centroids
why: With w ≈ 2 and 25 blocks, all dictionaries together weigh about 50 entries per layer — less than 2 % of a 4096-slot hot cache.
title: Q3: do misses concentrate in few, long-lived blocks?

q: Q3 can be answered without looking at a single KV value. Why?
a: It is about which positions are selected and how they group into blocks — a property of the selection trace
wrong: Because it only uses BF16 data
Because it is answered by a theorem
Because the answer is known from HiSparse
why: Which-versus-what. Q3 needs queries and positions (to replay selections), not the contents of entries.
title: Q3: do misses concentrate in few, long-lived blocks?

q: In framework A, what is varied?
a: The token distance Δ to the neighbour (and, in a second pass, the neighbour’s axis — one layer down)
why: Framework A holds the data, format, predictor and accounting fixed, and sweeps Δ = 1, 2, 4 … 32K.
title: Framework A: bits versus distance

q: Why is the curve framework A measures a lower bound on the information a neighbour carries?
a: It uses a cheap (affine or low-rank) predictor; a cleverer one could extract more
wrong: Because it uses the fixed-length rate
Because the shuffle control subtracts from it
why: Bits saved by a particular predictor ≤ the mutual information per element. A flat curve says a cheap dictionary cannot use the neighbour, not that the neighbour is useless to every coder.
title: Framework A: bits versus distance

q: The bits-saved curve decays with Δ and halves around Δ ≈ 350 tokens. What does that suggest?
a: Fallen-apple similarity, with a natural block scale of a few hundred tokens
why: A curve that fades with distance is the signature of local similarity; where it fades sets the block size.
title: Framework A: bits versus distance

q: What must happen to the distance curve after tokens are shuffled across sequences?
a: It must drop to (nearly) zero at every Δ
wrong: It must rise, because shuffling adds noise
why: Shuffling destroys every neighbour relationship. A gain that survives the shuffle is a bug, not similarity.
title: Framework A: bits versus distance

q: What are the two coordinates of a point on the compressibility curve?
a: Dictionary cost per entry (w/b, in entries’ worth) and delta size per entry (the delta ratio ρ)
wrong: Bits per element and token distance
why: Each setting of each algorithm, at one block size, lands at one (w/b, ρ) point. Their sum is the total storage per entry.
title: Framework B: the compressibility curve and its roofline

q: Where do HiSparse today and solo coding sit on the curve’s plane?
a: HiSparse at (0, 1); solo coding at (0, ≈ 0.78) with an ideal coder, (0, ≈ 0.88) fixed-length
wrong: They cannot be placed: they have no dictionary
why: Neither has a dictionary (x = 0). Raw entries are ρ = 1; a global context-free code is about 6.2 bits of 8 ideally, about 7 fixed-length.
title: Framework B: the compressibility curve and its roofline

q: What is the roofline?
a: The lower envelope of all the curves — the smallest delta any tried coder reaches at each dictionary budget
wrong: The upper bound on the miss rate
why: It is the practical, operational form of fallen-apple similarity at block scale. Theory says where it cannot go; the measurement says where it does go.
title: Framework B: the compressibility curve and its roofline

q: The roofline hugs the solo line everywhere. What is the verdict?
a: The block idea is dead; report the negative measurement and use context-free coding on the miss path
wrong: Lever 1 is alive with light dictionaries
why: No coder, at any dictionary cost, does better than coding each entry alone.
title: Framework B: the compressibility curve and its roofline

q: Why is framework B a machine for searching rather than a single experiment?
a: The space of coders is large, and a fixed interface and score let any new coder be placed on the same plot
wrong: Because the answer is already known from theory
Because only one coder can be lossless
Because it measures requests per GPU
why: VQ variants, transforms, rate allocation, residual coders — nobody can pick the winner from an armchair. One interface, one score, four controls.
title: Framework B: the compressibility curve and its roofline

q: What does framework C need from the model, and what does it not need?
a: It needs the selected positions at every step and layer; it does not need the contents of any entry
wrong: It needs the compressed deltas of every entry
It needs a working GPU decoder
It needs BF16 and FP8 copies of every key
why: Where misses land is a property of the selection trace — which entries — not of their bytes.
title: Framework C: where do misses land?

q: Which of these is a sanity check in framework C, rather than its main output?
a: The token miss rates at B = 2K, 4K, 8K, compared with HiSparse’s 30 / 13.4 / 6.7 %
wrong: The δ-miss fraction f_D for each number of resident dictionaries
The share of selections held by the heaviest blocks
why: The miss rates calibrate the proxy indexer against a real one; f_D, loads and block heaviness answer Q3.
title: Framework C: where do misses land?

q: In the toy replay, concentration is set to zero. The token miss rate stays near 15 %, but f_D drops. What does that show?
a: Re-selecting the same entries (Lucky Louis) does not by itself put the misses into few blocks
wrong: That the hot cache is broken
That more dictionaries always fix the problem
why: The toy indexer still re-selects most positions, so the hot cache works; but the selections are scattered, so misses touch many blocks.
title: Framework C: where do misses land?

q: Replay gives f_D = 0.85 with 4 resident dictionaries but 0.6 loads per step per layer. With heavy dictionaries (w = 256), is that affordable?
a: No — 0.6 × 256 ≈ 154 entries’ worth of loads per step, more than half the miss traffic it saves on
wrong: Yes, f_D above 0.8 is all that matters
Yes, loads are free because dictionaries are small
It cannot be judged without knowing ρ exactly
why: Loads must satisfy n_load · w ≪ 274. For w = 256 that means under about 0.1 per step per layer.
title: Framework C: where do misses land?

q: Where do the inputs ρ and f_D of the cost model come from?
a: ρ from framework B (the best affordable coder), f_D and n_load from framework C (trace replay)
wrong: Both are free parameters chosen to look good
why: Framework D has no measurement of its own; it combines B and C with the reference setting and sweeps the hardware.
title: Framework D: requests per GPU

q: Why compare each system at its own best hot-cache size B instead of at B = 4096?
a: HiSparse can also pick its B; a fixed-B comparison credits kv-blockdiff with gains HiSparse could get by retuning
wrong: Because B = 4096 is not a power of two
It makes no difference to the result
why: At B = 4096 the toy numbers give 109 versus 138 requests (1.26×); at each system’s own best B, 127 versus 141 (1.11×).
title: Framework D: requests per GPU

q: Making misses cheaper by a factor 1/ρ (lever 1 alone) raises requests per GPU by roughly…
a: The square root of 1/ρ, because the best B shrinks and the gain is shared between the link and the memory limits
why: N_link grows like B^1.08/ρ and N_HBM falls like 1/B; they meet at a B that scales like ρ^(1/2.08), so N scales like (1/ρ)^0.48.
title: Framework D: requests per GPU

q: According to the framework’s thresholds, what gain on the binding constraint is “not worth a system”?
a: Under about 1.1×
why: 1.3–2× is a strong systems result; under 1.1× the complexity is not repaid.
title: Framework D: requests per GPU

q: Why could the indexer’s keys be a dictionary “at zero marginal cost”?
a: They are already kept on the GPU for every token, because the indexer scores every past position at every step
wrong: Because they are stored in BF16
Because the indexer key is the same as the entry
Because indexer keys are never read
why: A predictor from indexer key to entry would be global (one per layer, shared by all requests); its input is already resident.
title: Parked: free and shared dictionaries

q: What makes a dictionary for a shared prompt prefix potentially free?
a: It is fit once and shared by every request that uses the prefix, so its cost is spread over many requests
wrong: Prefix caching compresses KV losslessly already
why: Amortization across requests instead of across entries. The open question is how many hot entries actually sit in shared blocks.
title: Parked: free and shared dictionaries

q: What is the main cost of using real “anchor” entries as the dictionary?
a: The sibling tax — the residual is the difference of two noisy vectors, so its noise doubles
wrong: Anchors must be fetched over the link on every miss
why: Predicting one noisy entry from another adds both noises. The bonus is that anchors are real entries attention can use as hits.
title: Parked: free and shared dictionaries

q: For rate allocation across channels, what decides whether it is cheap?
a: Whether the best allocation transfers across requests (then it is a global, free choice) or must be refit per block
wrong: Whether the GPU supports per-channel widths
Whether keys and values have the same size
why: A transferable allocation lives in a global dictionary; a per-block one costs dictionary bytes like any other block dictionary.
title: Parked: free and shared dictionaries

q: If upstairs similarity is strong and selections are shared across groups of 4 layers, what could be gained?
a: One dictionary per layer group instead of per layer — about 4× less residency
why: Layers that share both a selection and a dictionary need only one resident dictionary per group.
title: Parked: other neighbours and other splits

q: Why may the GQA-heads question not transfer to the real target models?
a: MLA models store one latent vector per token and layer — there is no head axis in the cache
wrong: Because GQA heads are always identical
Because heads are stored in BF16
why: The head axis exists in GQA caches like our proxy’s (2 key/value heads) but not in MLA caches.
title: Parked: other neighbours and other splits

q: What would it mean if missed entries compress worse than entries on average?
a: The miss path sees a harder distribution, so ρ on the miss path is worse than ρ measured on the whole history
wrong: The hot cache is too small
why: Entries that are surprising in time (they escape LRU) might also be surprising in content; the delta ratio that matters is the one of the missed entries.
title: Parked: other neighbours and other splits

q: Why is “prefill versus generated” slightly harder to measure than it looks with the wave-1 data?
a: The wave-1 dumps run the model over existing text; generated tokens need the model to actually write
wrong: Because generated tokens have no keys
Because prefill tokens are not cached
Because it needs a production trace
why: Treating the last part of a document as “decode” gives teacher-forced tokens, not tokens the model chose itself.
title: Parked: other neighbours and other splits

q: What makes an automated search over coders possible at all?
a: The measuring program has one interface, one score and fixed controls, so any proposed coder can be scored without a human
wrong: A large language model that knows the answer
why: A proposer writes a coder, the program scores it and draws its curve, a reviewer reads the curve and proposes the next one.
title: Parked: automated search and compressibility as a probe

q: An automated search reports a coder whose block-local gain survives shuffling. What is the most likely explanation?
a: A bug or a leak — block-local gains must vanish when neighbours are no longer neighbours
wrong: The shuffle was too weak to matter
why: That is exactly the cheat the shuffle control exists to catch.
title: Parked: automated search and compressibility as a probe

q: What would the per-layer distance curves tell us as a by-product?
a: Which layers hold slowly varying state and which hold token-by-token detail
wrong: Which layers can be removed from the model
why: A layer whose bits fade over thousands of tokens carries slow state; one whose bits vanish after a few tokens carries detail. Interpretability data, for free.
title: Parked: automated search and compressibility as a probe

q: What is the harness?
a: The small program that runs every dictionary algorithm through one interface, charges every byte by one rule, runs the controls and plots the results
wrong: A GPU kernel that decodes deltas at gather speed
The sparse-attention indexer of the proxy model
A test suite for the serving system
why: It is a referee, not a coder. Coders plug into it; it decides what their numbers are worth.
title: The harness: one interface

q: Two people report “1.4× on 8-bit KV”. Which difference makes the claims impossible to compare?
a: One charged the dictionary’s bytes to the entries that use it, the other did not
wrong: One used Python, the other C++
One ran on keys first, the other on values first
One printed the ratio, the other the bits per element
why: A dictionary that is not paid for makes any coder look good. The harness charges every byte by the same rule, so the numbers mean the same thing.
title: The harness: one interface

q: Which three methods does every algorithm implement in the harness?
a: fit (build the dictionary), encode (one delta per entry), decode (rebuild an entry bit for bit)
why: The harness supplies everything else: the byte counts, both rates and the controls.
title: The harness: one interface

q: Why must each delta be decodable alone, given only its dictionary?
a: Because a cache miss fetches one scattered entry; it cannot decode the entries before it first
wrong: Because Python cannot keep state between calls
Because it makes the deltas smaller
Because the dictionary changes after every entry
why: The access pattern of the miss path is random access. A stream coder that needs the previous entries would have to fetch them too.
title: The harness: one interface

q: Why does a fixed interface make an automated search over coders possible?
a: A proposer can write a new coder, and the harness scores it with the same rule and controls, with no human judging each claim
wrong: Because a fixed interface makes every coder equally fast
Because the controls choose the best coder by themselves
Because the interface forbids heavy dictionaries
why: One interface and one score turn “is this coder better?” into a number. The controls guard against the ways a search would cheat.
title: The harness: one interface

q: What are the three parts of a coder’s rate in bits per element?
a: Residual bits, the per-entry tax, and the dictionary’s bytes amortized over its block
wrong: Fit time, encode time and decode time
why: The dish, the service charge and the shared table: what the residual costs, what each entry pays for its own pointer or index, and 8w/b for the dictionary.
title: One accounting rule for every rung

q: A VQ codebook weighs w=256 entries’ worth. What does it cost per element at b=512?
a: 4 bits — half of the raw 8
why: 8w/b=8⋅256/512=4. No residual saving can pay for that; VQ needs blocks of 8K entries or more.
title: One accounting rule for every rung

q: Why does the harness report two rates for every point?
a: The entropy rate is what an ideal coder would reach; the fixed-length rate is what a fast random-access GPU format reaches
wrong: One is for keys and one is for values
One is in bits and the other in bytes
One includes the dictionary and the other does not
why: Both include every tax. They differ only in how the residuals are coded, and the gap between them is the price of random access.
title: One accounting rule for every rung

q: In the harness’s fixed-length format, how is an escaped element marked?
a: Its field holds the one value the width rule never uses, −2n−1, and its raw code follows the entry
wrong: By a separate list of positions in the block
By setting the field to zero
It is not marked; escapes are dropped
why: The width rule allows residuals with magnitude below 2n−1, so the most negative field value is free to mean “escaped”. An escape then costs its 8 raw bits and no position.
title: One accounting rule for every rung

q: Which scope gets its dictionary for free?
a: Global scope — it is fit once on separate calibration data and shared by every request
wrong: Block scope, because blocks are small
Request scope, because it is loaded once
None — every scope pays the same
why: A global dictionary costs nothing per request at serving time. Request and block dictionaries are paid by the entries that share them.
title: One accounting rule for every rung

q: What does the synthetic-truth control check?
a: That the harness recovers structure planted in generated data with a known answer
wrong: That real KV data is compressible
That the GPU decoder is fast enough
That the dictionary fits in HBM
why: If the gain does not peak at the planted block length, or does not match the float-domain measurement of the same sample, the method is broken before any real data arrives.
title: Four controls, built before any real data

q: After the shuffle control, which gain must vanish?
a: Every block-local gain — on the synthetic set, g_blk fell from 0.342 to −0.004 bit
wrong: Every gain, including the request-scope gain
why: Shuffling entries across sequences destroys neighbourhoods. A block dictionary has nothing local left to exploit; any block gain that survives is a bug or overfitting.
title: Four controls, built before any real data

q: On the synthetic set, the shuffled request gain stayed at about 0.13 bit. Why?
a: The global dictionary was fit on too few calibration sequences, so the evaluation data as a whole differs from it — a calibration gap, not request structure
wrong: The shuffle was not random enough
Request scope always gains 0.13 bit by definition
why: After the shuffle every “request” is a sample of the whole evaluation pool, and the pool’s average differs from the calibration data’s. More calibration sequences shrink the gap (0.22 → 0.12 → 0.07 bit for 2, 8, 32 sequences).
title: Four controls, built before any real data

q: What bug does the round-trip control catch that the rate numbers never would?
a: A lossy step: e.g. residuals computed in int8 wrap around (120 − (−100) becomes −36), so decoding gives the wrong code
wrong: A dictionary that is too big
A block size that is too small
Keys and values being mixed up
why: Rates are computed from the residuals; a wrapped residual is small and looks cheap. Only rebuilding the entry and comparing it bit by bit reveals that it is wrong.
title: Four controls, built before any real data

q: What does the scope-consistency control compare?
a: Request scope against block scope with b equal to the whole sequence — they must agree to the bit
wrong: The entropy rate against the fixed-length rate
why: The two code paths must describe the same thing. A dropped partial block or a different amortization denominator shows up as a difference.
title: Four controls, built before any real data

q: Which model’s KV cache does wave 1 measure?
a: The full-attention layers of a small open proxy model (Qwen3.5-2B), replicated on Qwen3-1.7B
wrong: The real sparse-attention target model, on a cluster
why: The real target does not fit the 16 GB GPU at hand. A small model with plain GQA attention is a clean place to measure neighbour similarity; whether it transfers is itself a risk (R6).
title: The data behind the harness

q: Why are keys stored before RoPE?
a: RoPE rotates channel pairs by a position-dependent angle, which smears the per-channel structure a dictionary would exploit; rotating after decoding is cheap
why: Before the rotation, a channel’s values sit around a stable location; after it, the same channel wobbles with position.
title: The data behind the harness

q: Why must the calibration set be disjoint from the evaluation set?
a: Otherwise the global dictionary has seen the test data, and global scope cheats
wrong: Because calibration data is in BF16
Because the calibration set is used for the shuffle control
why: Global scope is supposed to capture only what all texts share. Fitting it on the very sequences it codes turns it into a request dictionary that nobody paid for.
title: The data behind the harness

q: Roughly how much GPU memory does the Qwen3.5-2B dump need at 32K tokens?
a: About 5–6 GB — 4 GB of weights, 0.4 GB of KV, plus working memory
why: Only 6 of 24 layers keep a growing KV cache: 6×32768×1024×2 bytes ≈ 0.40 GB. The weights dominate.
title: The data behind the harness

q: How large is the whole wave-1 data set of 8-bit codes?
a: About 2 GB — 10 sequences × 32K tokens × 6 layers × 1 KB
why: An entry of the proxy model is 1024 elements, one byte each in 8 bits. 10×32768×6×1024 B ≈ 2.0 GB: it fits in RAM.
title: The data behind the harness

q: What exactly must the store reproduce bit for bit?
a: The 8-bit (E4M3 or INT8) codes of the KV cache, not the BF16 original
wrong: The float32 values before any rounding
why: The rounding to 8 bits is a separate, accepted step (where KV storage is heading anyway). The store’s promise starts after it.
title: Step 0: the exact 8-bit target

q: What is the E4M3 index of a value?
a: Its position among the representable values, counted from zero, with a sign — from −126 to 126
wrong: Its rank among the values of the block
why: In index space one step is one representable value, whatever its size. Conveniently, the index is the byte itself read as a sign-magnitude integer: 8 × exponent field + mantissa field.
title: Step 0: the exact 8-bit target

q: What bug did the source’s e4m3_round have?
a: It promised to turn −0 into +0, but returned −0.0 for tiny negative values
wrong: It rounded ties away from zero
why: sign(x) × 0 is −0.0 for negative x. The two compare equal in numpy, so the source’s own test passed; a bit-level comparison fails. Adding +0.0 fixes it.
title: Step 0: the exact 8-bit target

q: Why does a single Laplace bump in index space fit E4M3 codes badly?
a: A zero-centred channel’s E4M3 codes form two humps, one per sign, because the grid is dense near zero
wrong: Because E4M3 has fewer codes than INT8
Because the Laplace has no scale parameter
Because E4M3 values are always positive
why: On the log grid, values near zero spread over many tiny steps, so the codes pile up away from index 0 on both sides. On our synthetic set the index-space Laplace charges solo coding 8.4 bits — more than raw.
title: Step 0: the exact 8-bit target

q: On the synthetic set, how much of the scope gains survives in E4M3’s fixed-length rate?
a: About 0.22 bit, against 0.94 bit for INT8
wrong: All of it — the grid does not matter
why: With fixed-length fields, a residual counts grid steps; across zero the E4M3 grid is dense, so residuals are long. The entropy rate with a grid-aware model keeps ≈ 0.80 bit in both formats.
title: Step 0: the exact 8-bit target

q: Which three numbers does experiment 1a compute?
a: The distance curve (bits versus token distance), the location gain, and the KLT gain
wrong: The entropy rate, the fixed-length rate and the solo rate
The miss rate, the δ-miss fraction and the loads per step
why: All three are float-domain, grid-free numbers that bound what cheap dictionaries could save, before any coder exists.
title: Experiment 1a: the one-hour diagnostic

q: How does 1a turn the predictability of an entry from its neighbour at distance Δ into bits?
a: By the exchange rate 21​log2​1−R21​, with R2 the share of variance the best per-channel affine prediction explains
wrong: By the cosine similarity of the two entries
By the ratio of their norms
why: For Gaussian-like data, explaining a share R² of the variance leaves a residual of variance (1 − R²)σ², which saves exactly that many bits.
title: Experiment 1a: the one-hour diagnostic

q: What does a distance curve that is flat but clearly above zero at every Δ mean?
a: The structure is per-request or global, not local — informative for scope, but not fallen-apple similarity
wrong: Strong fallen-apple similarity at small Δ
why: Local similarity decays with distance. A level line says every entry of the sequence shares something, which a request or global dictionary already captures.
title: Experiment 1a: the one-hour diagnostic

q: After 1a, what reading means “Q1 is in serious trouble”?
a: Location gain plus KLT gain at block scope below 0.3 bit, on both keys and values
wrong: A KLT gain larger than the location gain
why: Cheap dictionaries could then save at most a third of a bit, before the 8-bit grid takes its share. Above 1 bit on keys, the project has a pulse.
title: Experiment 1a: the one-hour diagnostic

q: Why does experiment 1b follow even when 1a looks good?
a: Because the 8-bit grid can take back part of what float-domain numbers promise
why: On the synthetic set, the same structure is worth 0.80 bit in the entropy rate but only 0.22 bit in E4M3’s fixed-length rate.
title: Experiment 1a: the one-hour diagnostic

q: Which rungs does experiment 1b climb?
a: loc, the KLT bound, a rank-16 partial KLT, VQ with 256 centroids on 64-element pieces, and sib
why: Global, request and block are the scopes each rung is run at. The rungs are the dictionary types, from the lightest to the heaviest.
title: Experiment 1b: the exact lossless ladder

q: Why is a 256-centroid VQ codebook pointless at b=512 for 1024-element entries?
a: Its dictionary share 8w/b is about 4 bits per element, more than any plausible saving
wrong: Because k-means does not converge on 512 entries
Because 512 is not a power of two
why: 8×259/512≈4. The same codebook costs a quarter of a bit at 8K and 0.06 bit at request scope.
title: Experiment 1b: the exact lossless ladder

q: In the harness, what decides whether a dictionary is global, request or block scope?
a: Which fitting set the harness hands to fit() — calibration codes, the whole sequence, or the block itself
wrong: A scope flag inside each coder
Whether the coder is light or heavy
why: Coders never choose their scope. The harness chooses what they may see and who pays for the result.
title: Experiment 1b: the exact lossless ladder

q: On the synthetic set, why is solo coding’s fixed-length rate exactly 8.0 bits?
a: The plain fixed-length format cannot shorten raw 8-bit codes that use the whole range — a straw-man baseline
wrong: Because the synthetic data is random
Because the dictionary share is 8 bits
why: A zero-centred channel spans nearly all 255 codes, so its field needs 8 bits. A real solo baseline must split off the exponent, as SplitZip does, or the fixed-length gains look larger than they are.
title: Experiment 1b: the exact lossless ladder

q: Which wave-1 output answers Q1 most directly?
a: Figure A — bits saved against token distance, with its shuffled twin
why: The distance curve measures fallen-apple similarity itself; Table 1 and Figure B measure what coders make of it.
title: What wave 1 produces

q: What are the cells of Table 1?
a: Entropy rate and fixed-length rate of each dictionary type at global, request and best block scope
wrong: Miss rates at three hot-cache sizes
Compression ratios of zstd and gzip
why: From those cells come the two scope gains greq​ and gblk​ for the cheapest type that achieves them — the inputs of the decision rule.
title: What wave 1 produces

q: Which wave-1 number feeds the cost model of wave 2?
a: The delta ratio ρ (and delta size) of the fixed-length coder at the best affordable block size and dictionary weight
wrong: The entropy rate of solo coding
why: The fixed-length rate is the size of a real delta, so ρ≈bpe/8 of that coder is what a miss would move.
title: What wave 1 produces

q: How long is “one weekend” really, in the source’s own schedule?
a: Three days of work, plus an evening of dumping before
why: Day 1 builds and runs 1a, Day 2 runs 1b with VQ overnight, Day 3 reads and decides. Call it a long weekend.
title: What wave 1 produces

q: Why do the four controls sit in front of experiment 1b in the pipeline, not after it?
a: Because a control run after the results are known invites explaining a failure away
wrong: Because the controls need the 1b results as input
Because the controls run on the GPU
Because 1b is too slow to repeat
why: The controls must pass on synthetic data before real data enters the harness; they gate the measurement.
title: What wave 1 produces

q: What does the decision rule take as input?
a: The two scope gains greq​ and gblk​ of the best cheap dictionary type, keys and values byte-weighted, best of the two 8-bit grids
wrong: The miss rate of the hot cache
why: Wave 1’s Table 1 boils down to these two numbers; the rule maps them to what happens next.
title: The decision rule

q: Which outcome sends wave 2 to block scope?
a: greq​+gblk​≥0.75 bit and gblk​≥0.4 bit
wrong: gblk​<0.15
greq​≥0.75 alone
why: A large total, a good part of it local: fallen-apple similarity that is real and block-scale.
title: The decision rule

q: What does the source’s rule say for greq​=0.5, gblk​=0.3?
a: Nothing — the total is above 0.75 but the block gain lies between 0.15 and 0.4, a case no row covers
why: The first two rows need g_blk ≥ 0.4 or g_blk < 0.15. The band in between has no row. Our synthetic set lands in it.
title: The decision rule

q: Which rate should the rule be applied to, in our reading?
a: The fixed-length rate, with the entropy rate as the ceiling a better format could reach
why: The fixed-length rate is the size of the delta a miss would actually move. The source’s rule does not say which rate it means.
title: The decision rule

q: The same synthetic data, read in E4M3’s fixed-length rate, gives 0.058 + 0.161 bit. Which row?
a: The negative row — below 0.25 bit in total
why: In INT8’s entropy rate the same data gives 0.80 bit and lands in the gap. Which grid and which rate the rule reads matters as much as its thresholds.
title: The decision rule

q: How does wave 2 get sparse selections from a model without a trained indexer?
a: It takes the exact attention ranking — for each decode step and layer, the top-k positions by attention probability summed over heads
wrong: It trains a DSA indexer on the proxy model
It selects the k most recent tokens
why: The DSA indexer is trained to approximate attention’s own ranking, so the exact ranking is a fair stand-in for block-level statistics.
title: Wave 2: simulating the indexer

q: What is trace replay?
a: Recording the selection of every decode step, then re-running the hot cache and the dictionary cache on that list
wrong: Replaying the network traffic of a server
Decoding the deltas a second time to check them
why: Caches only need to know which entries are wanted, in which order. A recorded trace lets every cache size and policy be tried without a GPU kernel.
title: Wave 2: simulating the indexer

q: In the replay, when is a miss counted as a δ-miss?
a: When the dictionary of the missed entry’s block is already resident at the moment of the miss
wrong: When the entry was ever in the hot cache before
When the block is among the heaviest after the step
Always, if the block has a dictionary
why: Dictionaries are loaded after the step’s misses, for future steps. A miss is cheap only if its dictionary was already on the GPU.
title: Wave 2: simulating the indexer

q: What did the source’s replay code leave undefined?
a: The residency policy — the function choosing which block dictionaries to keep (top_blocks_by_resident_count)
wrong: The block index of a position
why: The harness implements two policies — the heaviest blocks in the hot cache, and an LRU of blocks hit by a miss — because the policy is what framework C compares.
title: Wave 2: simulating the indexer

q: Why does wave 2 first measure token miss rates at B = 2K, 4K and 8K?
a: As a sanity check — they should land near HiSparse’s 30 %, 13 % and 7 %; if not, the proxy indexer is more or less local than DSA’s
wrong: Because they decide the block size
Because the cost model ignores them
why: Exact top-k on a 2B model is a stand-in. Comparing its miss rates with HiSparse’s published ones says how far to trust its block statistics.
title: Wave 2: what to measure

q: Which reading of framework C says heavy per-block dictionaries are affordable?
a: A δ-miss fraction of at least 0.8 with at most 8 resident dictionaries, and at most 0.1 loads per step
why: Most misses then find their dictionary on the GPU, and loading a 256-entry dictionary every ten steps or less stays small next to ~274 misses per layer per step.
title: Wave 2: what to measure

q: When is framework C moot?
a: When wave 1 says light dictionaries (w ≈ 2–4) suffice — they are all resident anyway
wrong: When the hot cache is large
When the miss rate is above 30 %
why: A dictionary a few entries’ worth in size costs almost nothing to keep for every block, so where misses land no longer matters.
title: Wave 2: what to measure

q: In the synthetic replay sweep, what happens to f_D as more dictionaries are kept resident?
a: It rises — more of the misses find their block’s dictionary already on the GPU — while the loads per step change with the policy
wrong: It falls, because the cache thrashes
why: f_D is the share of misses whose dictionary is resident; keeping more dictionaries can only help, at the price of HBM.
title: Wave 2: what to measure

q: In the reference setting, how many requests per GPU does HiSparse serve at B = 4K, and what binds?
a: About 109, bound by the link
why: 13.7 MB of misses per request per step against 1.5 GB per 30 ms step over a 50 GB/s link gives 109; HBM alone would allow 146.
title: The cost model, and the paper in every outcome

q: A request-scope dictionary with ρ = 0.75 and w = 256: requests per GPU at 50 GB/s?
a: About 138 — now bound by HBM, a gain of about 1.26×
why: Cheaper misses lift the link bound to 146, but the dictionaries add HBM, which now binds at 138.
title: The cost model, and the paper in every outcome

q: Which gain on the binding constraint does framework D call “not worth a system”?
a: Under 1.1×
why: A 1.3–2× gain on the binding constraint is a strong systems result; under 1.1× the engineering is not worth it.
title: The cost model, and the paper in every outcome

q: If Q1 comes out negative, what is the paper?
a: “How much conditional structure is left in 8-bit KV caches? (Not much.)” — a shuffle-controlled measurement with a BF16 column and an E4M3-versus-INT8 comparison
wrong: The same systems paper with smaller numbers
A paper on a new sparse-attention indexer
why: No lossless number for KV neighbour similarity exists anywhere; a careful “no” redirects the field to context-free miss-path coding.
title: The cost model, and the paper in every outcome

q: Why does wave 1 target 8-bit storage rather than BF16?
a: KV storage is converging on 8 bits, and BF16’s low bits carry noise that makes lossless coding a different, less relevant problem
wrong: Because BF16 cannot be coded losslessly
Because the GPU cannot read BF16
why: The direction is solid; the format is not — E4M3 and INT8 behave differently under prediction, so both are scored.
title: Fixed choices and their assumptions

q: Why is exact top-k attention an acceptable stand-in for the DSA indexer?
a: The indexer is trained to approximate attention’s ranking, so block-level statistics should carry over, though exact miss rates will differ
wrong: Because the indexer does not affect misses
Because HiSparse does not use an indexer
why: Reasonable for concentration statistics; the miss rates are calibrated against HiSparse’s published ones.
title: Fixed choices and their assumptions

q: The source rated the residual coders “safe”. Why does the harness disagree on E4M3?
a: The index-space Laplace model charges E4M3 solo coding more than raw (8.4 bits on synthetic data); a grid-aware model is needed
wrong: Because Laplace models cannot be fit on 8-bit data
Because entropy coders are too slow
why: E4M3 codes of a zero-centred channel form two humps that one index-space bump cannot describe.
title: Fixed choices and their assumptions

q: Which choice would we change first, before any real data?
a: The number of calibration sequences — from 2 to at least 8, better 32
why: With 2 calibration sequences the synthetic shuffle control shows a 0.22-bit calibration gap in the request gain; the dump cost of more is tiny.
title: Fixed choices and their assumptions

q: Why can wave 1 ignore speculative decoding and multi-token prediction?
a: They change how many selections happen per step, not what one miss costs
wrong: Because they make KV caches smaller
why: The coder works per entry; more selections per step scale the traffic, not the delta size.
title: Ignored on purpose

q: Why is a block-scaled number format (shared exponents per block) not a new problem?
a: A per-block scale is just another tiny dictionary — about two bytes per block
wrong: Because GPUs do not support it
why: The same accounting applies; the scale is charged like any other dictionary byte.
title: Ignored on purpose

q: Why are better eviction policies left out?
a: They are bounded — Bélády’s optimum is only a few points better than LRU — and orthogonal to coding
wrong: Because eviction does not affect misses
Because they need a GPU kernel
why: Even a perfect eviction policy would leave most misses; cheaper misses help whichever policy is used.
title: Ignored on purpose

q: Which ignored item is the riskiest, in our reading?
a: MLA latents — the real target — which are already a learned low-rank projection, so the transform rungs may find less there
why: The ladder applies unchanged, but the statistics may not transfer. That is a measurement, scheduled for later.
title: Ignored on purpose

q: What must exist before the victim tier and lever 2 proper are built?
a: A decode kernel with measured throughput — and a “go” from waves 1 and 2
why: Both put the decoder on the critical path of attention; its speed must be known first.
title: Ignored on purpose

q: What is the pivot if 8-bit KV turns out to have no usable conditional structure (R1)?
a: Publish the negative with the BF16 column, and build a global fixed-length coder for the miss path — solo coding for sparse decode
wrong: Use bigger blocks until a gain appears
why: Solo coding is worth ~1.1–1.3× for free and needs no residency; the negative measurement is new on its own.
title: Weak spots, risks and pivots

q: How would we know that gains exist only at request scope (R3)?
a: From Table 1: gblk​ is small while greq​ is not
why: The pivot is “requestdiff”: one dictionary per request per layer, no dictionary cache. Simpler, still new.
title: Weak spots, risks and pivots

q: Which risk can only be checked in phase 2, not in wave 1 or 2?
a: R8 — that the decoder cannot run at gather speed
wrong: R3 — gains only at request scope
why: Throughput needs a kernel. Until then, the fixed-length rate predicts the format a fast decoder would read.
title: Weak spots, risks and pivots

q: Where is the argument thinnest, according to the source?
a: The prior on fallen-apple similarity (intuition plus lossy-literature hints), and the economics built on assumed ρ, w and f_D
why: There is no lossless number anywhere — which is both the risk and the reason the measurement is worth publishing either way.
title: Weak spots, risks and pivots

q: What third thin spot did building the harness add?
a: The engineering number — on synthetic data the E4M3 fixed-length rate kept 0.22 bit of a 0.80-bit structure, against a straw-man solo baseline
wrong: The entropy rate is always optimistic by 2 bits
why: What a fast format can cash in may be much less than what the data contains, and the fixed-length column still lacks a fair baseline.
title: Weak spots, risks and pivots

q: In one sentence, what does kv-blockdiff propose?
a: Store the KV history as per-block dictionaries plus tiny per-entry deltas, so a hot-cache miss moves a delta instead of a raw entry and the GPU rebuilds the entry exactly
wrong: Quantize the KV cache to fewer bits per value
Drop the least important tokens from the cache
Retrain the model to need a smaller cache
why: It is lossless and invisible to the model; only the bytes moved and stored change.
title: The one-page summary

q: Which property of KV caches must hold for the idea to pay off, and is it measured yet?
a: Fallen-apple similarity — an entry is cheaper to code given nearby entries — and no, not at 8-bit precision
wrong: The Lucky Louis property — and yes, HiSparse measured it
Upstairs similarity — and yes, KVQuant measured it
Perplexity — and yes, every model card reports it
why: The Lucky Louis property (selections repeat) is established, but it is about which entries are wanted, not about their bytes.
title: The one-page summary

q: How much variance must a dictionary explain to save one bit per element (Gaussian exchange rate)?
a: 75 % of the variance that remains after solo coding
why: Bits saved = ½ log₂ 1/(1−R²); R² = 0.75 gives exactly 1 bit; 94 % gives 2 bits.
title: The one-page summary

q: What is the go / no-go threshold of wave 1?
a: Request-scope plus block-scope gain of at least 0.75 bit per element → go; under 0.25 bit everywhere → publish the negative and pivot
why: The split between the two gains then decides block-scope versus request-scope dictionaries.
title: The one-page summary

q: Which three LRU miss rates did HiSparse measure on its GLM-5.1 trace, at hot-cache sizes 2048 (top-k only), 4096 and 8192?
why: Bélády’s clairvoyant policy at 4096 misses 8.2 %, so better eviction can win at most ~5 points.
title: Grounded numbers and their sources

q: What compression ratio does lossless exponent coding (SplitZip) report on BF16 KV caches?
a: About 1.32×
why: The mantissa bits are close to noise; only the exponent carries the easy, context-free redundancy.
title: Grounded numbers and their sources

q: How many distinct non-negative values does FP8 E4M3 (the “fn” variant) represent?
a: 127 — zero, 7 subnormals and 15 binades of 8 values, minus the one NaN pattern
why: With the sign, that is 253 distinct values plus −0, which we canonicalize to +0.
title: FP8 E4M3 facts used by the coder

q: Why does the coder work in “index space”?
a: So that a residual of 1 means one representable step, whatever the size of the step
wrong: Because indices are always smaller than values
Because E4M3 has no negative numbers
why: On a logarithmic grid, equal value differences are very different numbers of steps near zero and far from it.
title: FP8 E4M3 facts used by the coder

q: Which of the related works is lossless AND targets the sparse-decode miss path with random access?
a: None of them — that combination is what would be new
why: SplitZip is lossless but bulk and context-free; KVTC and CacheGen are lossy; HiSparse moves raw entries.
title: Prior-art map

q: Which classic results formalize “the receiver already has side information”?
a: Slepian–Wolf (1973) and Wyner–Ziv (1976)
why: Mattson’s stack distances and Bélády’s policy are about caches; Huffman is about prefix codes.
title: References
